instruction:
You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: There needs to be more to do in the quiet hours. There needs to be a marked plan for activities like walking (planned, measured routes), tours of the plant spaces, anything so that those of us kept in while Doctors tried to figure out what was wrong could do something. My case was clearly one of the 'cure is worse than the disease'. I continued to lose weight for 7-8 days after release. There has been no relapse of what they believed was a Gall Bladder attack, but my gastrointestinal tract is not the same as it was before. The fever that I presented with was suppressed until I told nurses to stop giving me Tylenol, so I could run a fever - they were wholly opposed to it, but that is what ultimately cleared the illness and the pain! This fear of fever cost me at least three days incarcerated. They did not seem to pay attention to the fact that I had felt so bloated in the days before it felt as if my belly button was tearing free. Their focus was all on my initial reports of pain, which were actually an evolution of the gas pains. I almost left the hospital for a real meal after miscommunication left me with another 'clear liquid' torture meal. I also walked out the doors unaccompanied by any staff - the nurses were busy, my spouse had come home from work at lunch, and I told the nurses not to bother. Something is still not right, but I do not expect the clinicians at XXXX to be able to diagnose it correctly. Essentially their plan is to remove the gallbladder to remove a variable - which is simply retarded from a diagnostic stand point (I do technical investigations, and that would never fly for a client - you don't just pull parts and hope something reveals itself)! I won't go into the fact that the O2 regulator at the head of my bed leaked for 2+ days before a new nurse came with a new one and installed it just moments before the maintenance man did (and almost replaced it again). I can only guess how much O2 was wasted, whether it was access to the part, or lack of training to isolate the line is unknown, but again at the very least it should have been turned off elsewhere.

input: I was diagnosed with cellulitis in my right thumb & hand A surgery/procedure was done & then I was admitted to the hospital. The internal medicine doctor released me that evening without conferring with the surgeon When I was released someone told me to keep taking my oral antibiotics for 7 days & if there was no improvement after the 7 days to come back to emergency The evening of my release the surgeon called my home to tell me that he was concerned that I had been released, as the surgical team (2 doctors) wanted to keep an eye on my thumb & whether the I&D worked. He asked what I had been told to do when I was released & I told him about being told to take my antibiotics for 7 days & to come back if there was no improvement He was incensed at this directive & told me that if there was no improvement in a day or 2 to get back to emerg. I ended up going back to emerg 2 days later & the attending doctor there decided I needed to go on a stronger IV antibiotic for 7 days - if it wasn't for the surgeon calling me I may have lost my thumb This was very back lack of communication between the surgeon & the internal medicine team on the I don't know who the young man was who told me to take the oral antibiotics for 7 days - but he was ill-informed - and I credit the surgeon who called me with saving my thumb/hand & maybe even my life SO that experience at XXXXXXXX was not good!!!

input: The nursing staff and doctors were all very kind and treated me with courtesy. I believe they all tried their best. However I found that at night time the service seemed overloaded and short staffed or something. After ringing bell over 3 times within a 45 minutes, I still could not get help to be disconnected from BP monitor and eventually I did it myself on 3 occasions between midnight and 7 AM. The washrooms facilities during these hours were not cleaned as far as I could judge. First cleaning was done after 8 AM. Breakfast or any food was only brought over after a request by 10 AM. Even though there was a room admission order for me, I was never admitted and possibly would not have been admitted until much later in the day. I went home a 1 PM. It is my opinion that the nursing staff is left with too much to cope with too few and some improvements are needed. In the last 7 years I had to stay overnight twice at the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and found that in general things were running in a smoother manner and the service was somehow better with more nurses available.

input: Yes I was taken to hospital by ambulance and I am still waiting for the bill The last time I went it was right at the height of COVID and I never received the bill until finally I got a call from a collection agency and I wish they will bill my insurance for the hospital stay Why won't they bill my insurance for the ambulance That doesn't make sense to me They obviously bill my insurance company for private coverage and anything the government doesn't cover but they won't bill them for the ambulance It's the hospital billing me for the ambulance So it's now a month and I still don't have the ambulance bill I wait for it every day hoping it will come and then I would have to send it on to my insurance company but last time I didn't get the ill and it went to a collection agency which was a novel experience for me I've never had anything like that. input: I found one of the nurses who cared for us to be really quite angry with her situation of shift work at the time. She gave me a lot of detail about how she is working multiple shifts with no days off. I also found her not very gentle with my son when she assessed him and proceeded with his COVID test (in both nostrils - which I did not think was necessary as all of my tests have only been 1 nostril, but I am not a medical professional). During the COVID test it took 3 nurses to hold my son down as he was thrashing a lot. The test of both nostrils caused trauma and he bled profusely from his nose, plus he ended up bursting blood vessels around both eyes with his crying. The nurse was not sympathetic to this and barely gave us a tissue to catch all the bleeding. She just kept saying she does this all day long and he has to endure it. I also found it would be approximately an hour between someone coming to our room. We were there for a total of 8 hours and I pressed the call button a few times to ask if we could leave to go to the bathroom or get some water and each time they would say someone would come to assist us but another hour would go by and no one would. The hospital was not busy this day as we waited almost no time to get a room but the service supplied by the nurses was below par.

input: I went to the hospital because of an appendicitis. It took staff almost 11 hours to confirm this. The day staff (doctors and nurses) were unprofessional. I did not even know who the actual doctor was in the emerg. Nurses were talking about other colleague in a negative manner (i.e. gossip) Lastly, the day nurses forgot to administer the barium solution to me before sending me for a CT scan. To be honest, I was in so much pain, that I forgot to record the nurse's names in order to file a complaint. In my opinion, they should be fired - they have no business to be taking care of sick people. On a positive notes, once there was a shift change the evening nurses and doctor (Dr. XXXX) and surgeon (Dr. XXXXXXX and his team in the OR) were excellent! What is most unfortunate is that my effort in completing this survey and writing down my experience will not change a thing at XXXXXXXXXXXX or in any XXXXXXX hospital/healthcare facility. Sincerely, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I attended the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. I was brought there via a police car with two policemen, due to my Youth Hab therapist showing concern for my suicidal thoughts. I was greeted and taken care of by the policemen who never left my side until the doctor was by my side. When I first got there they took my blood pressure and my heart rate was at 150 BPM, my blood pressure was also high. I set the alarm off, but they brushed it off as nothing and turned the alarm off. Keep in mind I was already there for over 30 mins, just sitting and waiting, why would my heart rate be at 150 BPM from sitting down? They may have just thought it was anxiety causing my heart to race. Though I have expressed concerns for my heart and have been on a heart monitor before, I am also only XX years old. After talking with the crisis hotline, which they were so generous. I saw the doctor only for him to tell me that I needed to 'handle my anxiety better'. The policemen were more concerned and showed more care than the doctor did, the policemen even called me the next day to check up on how I was doing and I waited over an hour and a half to talk to a doctor for him to tell me something I already know. I am writing this because when he told me that, I felt stupid for even being at the hospital for that reason, I was disgusted in myself, I felt ashamed. I would never ever suggest my friend to ever go see that doctor because they would ultimately just make their suicidal thoughts even worse, like he did me, I left feeling worse than when I got there. It was the policemen who helped me not the doctor. I got there shortly after 3 pm and didn't end up leaving until close to 7:30 pm.

input: For the task indicated in the letter I do not have a note made on the calendar so this was an unscheduled appointment probably to do with my catheter. I had a turp operation on XXXXX but prior to that I had numerous occasions to go to the hospital because of catheter problems usually. When taken into the emergency department, a nurse attended to me immediately, but since I already knew the problem, it seemed to take a long time for the correctional service. Also, when it comes ot inserting catheters, some nurses are  better at it than others. I had two painful experiences. On the first occasion, a nurse tried 3 times, the resident tried once + then a cardiologist doctor tried twice before  success. On the other occasion, the nurses gave up and called Dr. XXXXX at about 10pm he had problems but left the room for a few minutes + when he came back the catheter slid in painlessly. I asked the nurses about this but they said 'well he is a doctor'. I don't care what he is, if he has a special painless procedure, it should be shared.

input: a) Experience unprofessional change of room from private to semi-private with no prior notification or or explanation for the reason. Once in the new room, the patient in the other bed was very noisy. She and her husband talked loud non-stop as if there was no one else in the room. They had a visitor and the room was like at a fish market. No consideration for the ill whatsoever. There should be reminder signs up in the bedroom to ask patients and their visitors to lower their voice. Nurses should also remind them if she hears them talk loudly instead of joining them! I just barely recovered from a fever but could not rest since the room change. My bp was up, so was my temperature and I almost had a nervous breakdown. It was horrendous. Thanks goodness in the end, after being in tears, I was given a private room again. This incident could have resulted in my having to recover in hospital much longer because I was not allowed the appropriate rest quiet time. b) I was told the imaging was to be at 2pm but it did not happen until 6-7pm. I was supposed to eat lunch after the procedure but ended up not eating at all since I was told it could occur any minute. The imaging technician for my MRI was a young Chinese girl. I was helped by one other tech to get on the examination table but when the mri was finished, the tech girl was alone. I refused to let her push me as I had a peridural in my back (it was on hold). I asked her to pull me instead so that I could be helped from her table onto the roller bed. This is how all other nurses/people have been helping me get up so far and that way, I could also be in control rather than being pushed from behind where I could not have appropriate control of my bending on my abdomen (where I had surgery cut). She was annoyed that I was reluctant to let her push me and told me that she did it all the time and it was either that or I was on my own. In the end, I let her push me but it was quite painful. She acted annoyed that I dared telling her that I preferred to be pulled rather than being pushed. She rolled me quickly out into the hallway and left me hanging dry there like an unattended piece of meat for a good 30-45 mins. I had no access to my pain pump button as it was hung very high up. Also, my bladder was full but there was no way to get any help either. I raised my voice trying to get some help as soon as I heard people in the hallway above my head but no one came. I am sure that the tech heard me because I was besides the imaging room and the door was wide open but she just chose deliberately to ignore me. There was no other patient in the room after me. I almost had to urinate in my own bed. I felt treated with a big lack of dignity, like a corpse in the cold hallway. c) the hospital discharge time/day was not clearly decided, nor communicated to me and my partner. It was overnite when I needed help to go to the bathroom that I found out that I was to get discharged in the morning, The nurse who came in told me that I'd better be able move on my own as I was going to be discharged. She left me to do everything on my own unattended, It took me about half an hour to get to the bowl. I could have fallen along and no one would have known as the nurse did not even attend my first trial on my own. She acted as if annoyed by my asking to be helped and went out. It was ok if I had to try on my own but she could have stayed by my sides to give me a hand if I ever needed it. That was a dangerous trial, I was quite afraid of falling. Basically, I felt I was rushed out of the hospital without the appropriate preparation, nor notification, nor was the prescribed amount of my pain pills correct. I am a hospital pharmacist myself and that made me very anxious. The intern I talked to could not understand what I was explaining to her and I finally had to refuse to get discharged until I could see my attending physician in the evening. The worst would have been to get discharged anot have enough pills to control my pain which would have made me end up having to return to the hospital as no other outpatient dr would prescribe narcs. I finally got the correct number of pills and went home reassured only the morning after. I am a pharmacist and medication is my specialty but there is obviously some improvement to be made at discharge time, maybe involving a pharmacist would be a good idea instead of leaving the intern to handle the medication issue as she knew very little about weaning off pain medications. d) After I was forced to change from private to semi-private, the nurse did not attend my requests to my going to the bathroom in a timely manner. Not only I had to deal with my neighbour patient's noise, I had to wait quite a long time for the nurse and the bathroom was so far away, with barely any space to move my walker. It was very difficult to reach the bathroom altogether. This whole day spent stressing out delayed my recovery period and it was another wasted day in hospital. It could have been better if I was left in my private room to rest and started my recovering with enough space to walk around in my own room instead of being tied in bed listening to all the noisy discussions from the patient next door.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I would just like to comment on the apparent practice of administering blood thinners to everyone who is assigned to a bed. Although I had a saline IV attached to me, I was not immobilized and got up to use the restroom and walk around when I felt like it. If I did not ask questions, a nurse would have put a blood thinner in my IV for no reason! Just so that you understand my particular situation, I came into the ER XXXXXXXX evening, was sent home with an appt to come back in the morning for a CT scan. After the results came back I was brought to ER again. I went through the various ER depts for blood etc and it was determined that I should be admitted. There were no beds available so I stayed in the hallway overnight until the next morning. The surgeon determined that I could go home with antibiotics so really didn't need a room after all. Why, after barely 1 day of hanging around the ER, would I need a blood thinner? I think this practice should be re -evaluated. It's certainly not good for our health and it's an unnecessary cost that the pharmaceutical companies are charging to an already burdened health care system. Thank you

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: From attachment - To Whom it May Concern: In reference to my recent hospital experience, I arrived at the hospital emergency department around 8:00 PM on XXXXXXXX with excruciating pain. I explained to the traige nurse that I had an episode with similar pain two years prior and it was diagnosed as Appendicitis. The surgeon at the time treated it with antibiotics, without surgery. She told me to take a seat in the waiting room, but I paced the floor as I couldn't sit much because of the pain. After hours of waiting, I complained to the Traige nurse that the pain was intense and I needed to see a doctor soon. Her response was "other people are in pain as well, you'll have to wait your turn". During my long wait, I complained again, and was told patients were being seen according to priority. Meanwhile, I saw many patients being called in with colds, most of which were children, and many came in after me. I was very upset, and pointed out repeatedly that there was a possibility that I had Appendicitis, but to no avail. After five and half hours, I was finally called in to see doctor. The doctor proceeded to run the necessary tests and ordered a CT scan. I needed to lay down because of the intense pain, but again I was given a chair and I continued to pace the floors. I was told there was no available beds, but I saw two empty beds near the nurse's station, that were empty for some time. Finally around 4:00 AM I was diagnosed with Appendicitis and was given one of those same beds. I spoke to the surgeon on call at 8:00 AM who told me that he would do his best to squeeze me into his schedule of surgeries. I was taken to a room when it became available around 1:00 PM But when the nurses asked me to transfer over onto the other bed, I suddenly felt a more intense pain in my abdomen even worse that the one I was already feeling. I could barely speak from the pain, but I managed to tell them that something had changed. The pain was worse and that I thought something was wrong. No one seemed too concerned. I laid there all afternoon until I was taken to surgery at 5:30 PM where they found that my appendix had ruptured and they found a "mess" inside me. The surgeon was very skilled and still managed to do it laparoscopically. Thankfully, I recovered without infection or other complications, but it was quite an ordeal and I had to deal with the consequences of having had a ruptured appendix. I am extremely sensitive to prescription medications, so in order to somewhat tolerate the antibiotics, I was unable to take the pain medications as needed, resulting in poor pain control. The surgical floor nurses, and aids were extremely helpful, courteous and very hard working. I have nothing but praise for them and for the doctors who cared for me. But I feel that having had to wait for almost twenty four hours with Appendicitis, in excruciating pain, resulted in the perforation. My life was put in danger by a total disregard of the severity of my condition. I believe this was possibly avoidable, and totally unacceptable. I truly hope no-one else is made to experience as I went through. But with our health care system as it is today, I highly doubt it. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

input: I do realize that it is a wait system which depends on priority care which is understandable, and I respectfully and totally agree with this system. However, myself and another young boy both had cuts to our fingers and it is my understanding that if stitches are required it is a two hour window to receive stitches. Because of the nature of my cut it was treated with glue and I am unsure of the young boy's results. It would be ideal if minor injuries like mine could be dealt with in a quick manner by a nurse so these minor but necessary visits do not take up space in the waiting room or take up a doctors time away from patients with more serious health problems.

- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.

- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.

- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

input: The room I was in had black slimy bugs in the bathroom and also near my bed. My wife stopped coming to visit me so much due to that and when she did come she would not put her feet on the floor as the bugs move so fast they could get into her open toed shoes. The nurses said they have them all the time. Something about the shower drain is where they come up from. Then they clean the floor and they are gone for a while. Also,every time I wanted coffee I would get tea which I do not like. I would ask, even write notes to the kitchen, but still got tea, till the last couple of weeks I was there. Then I got my coffee. Other than these 2 items everything was satisfactory.

input: This was a follow up to two other trips to Emergency. First with some pain. Was diagnosed and told I would be staying overnight. Another doctor released me to go home with prescription. A call within 36 hours to come to emergency as test results were in had me go to emergency the second time, I was held overnight for observation and released that next day. The attending doctor had me return for the third time to retest blood and he gave me a prescription for bladder infection, blood infection. There was some discussion about E-Coli. Released after bloodwork results. I am happy with the results. Please with the professionalism and courtesy of the staff.

input: The doctor literally forgot I was waiting. Two weeks later I am still in excruciating pain but I don't have time to take off work and go to a doctor. I was hit by a car and my entire lower leg was swollen including my foot. He didn't even ask me to take off my sock, nor did he order an X-ray of my foot. I was given Ibuprofen for pain and told 'oh, well, you can walk' when I asked if I should be using a brace or something to support my leg. I suspect I have a fractured metatarsal but I guess we'll never know. I am still in so much pain I can't sleep more than 3-4 hours. I have a fairly high pain tolerance so I wasn't crying or carrying on in the ER, but maybe I would have gotten reasonable care if I'd put on a bit of a show.

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

They kept telling me that I need to go somewhere I had to go up and down by walking. It shouldn't be like that. They should ask me before my surgery. They did not even notify my parents that I was going to have a surgery. They just did it. Also they did not ask me Do you want to authorize these belongings to your parents? They couldn't just do everything as they please. I'm paying for my insurance and tax so I shouldn't be treated like that. Also I'm a girl young 6 months pregnant with excruciating pain. I'm due next month and if my delivery doesn't go well I will complain or sue. I will fight for my newborn baby. Also after I got discharged from the hospital after my surgery I got itchiness. I never had this problem before. My mom told me I had redness and scratches on my back. MY OB prescribed me an allergy medicine but I was trying to do home remedy and now its getting better.

input: overlooked this is concerning considering there was unexpected extra bleeding after delivery. Once again- we had some excellent nurses and doctors who were very diligent with their care. However, there was plenty of turnover on the postpartum floor and the ball was dropped. I returned home with not enough information to properly care for my condition. Luckily I have resources at my finger tips and was able to get by. Not everyone has this type of support though. Although I have high regard for certain doctors and nurses who cared for me, I was very disappointed in XXXXXXXXXXX overall.My labor experience with my nurse was excellent- I had one primary nurse the majority of the time, and she was very thorough and considerate with her care. During the delivery there was a team of doctors (resident, fellow, med student, nurses). I expected this and was fine with the number of people, however it was evident to my husband and me that the team was not all on the same page. The fellow did not seem to support the assessments and decisions of the resident (resident was taking lead), and there was quite a bit of back and forth to decide on a course of action. As a patient, it was unsettling to pick up on the negative feelings between doctors. I could tell that one doctor did not support the decision of another- this did not give me confidence. My baby had to be vacuumed, which resulted in a bad hematoma. I know this is a condition that can occur with vacuuming, but on the postpartum floor I had 3 different doctors and nurses make comments that the hematoma did not look good, and 'someone should have a talk with that doctor'. Based on family members who are L&D nurses, I have learnt that some hematomas can be avoid or the severity reduced based on the care of the doctor (removing the vacuum in between contractions). From the reactions of the XXXXXXXXXXX staff in the postpartum floor, I am assuming that the doctor that night was not careful enough. I sustained severe tearing during the delivery. The lead doctor (resident) briefed me on the tear just after my baby was delivered. I took in half the information because I was still in a state of shock from the arrival of my baby, and I assumed that surely that was not going to be the only time I was given information about my condition. Unfortunately that was the case- I was in the hospital about 48 hours after giving birth and no one fully briefed me on the type of tear nor provided thorough care instructions. A nurse did show my house to use the peri bottle and ice the area for 24 hours, but no instructions were given about mobility, signs to watch for, or guidance for a proper recovery. Another women on the postpartum floor had a severe tear as well and her doctors and nurses provided much more guidance- she encouraged me to ask about sitz baths, a sitting ring, and side-lying breast feeding. It seems our care varied drastically. On the post partum floor I had a few different nurses. Some were excellent, but two were did the bare minimum. Unfortunately the latter two were taking care of me during key moments- my arrival on the floor and my last morning. input: With the exception of 1 student nurse everybody who changed the bag from my catheter caused me great pain even after notifying them to please not tug on the catheter because of the pain it gave me. Nobody explained to me my catheter could become plugged so I just assumed the pain was normal when it happened to me. I was left lying in my own bloody urine after getting and irrigation for a blocked catheter which spilled all over my groin and wet the sheets on my bed the fand developed a rash on my skin. I also was not offered any way to clean myself as my IV and catheter drip were attached to the bed leaving me stuck to the bed without being able to shower. The nurses on night shift were always making so much noise it was IMPOSSIBLE to sleep. The food service personnel were friendly and helpful but the food is horrible tasting and mostly inedible. I was in a semi private room and me and my room mate had to wait long periods of time for a nurse to show after calling for one and often had to call multiple times. I would not go back for any procedure ever again.

input: The day after surgery I am on pain killers and not completely coherent. The physio therapist comes in and explains the exercises, a couple of people - not sure who they were tells me that CCAC will give me instructions on how to take care of myself. Are you kidding me? I am high and do not remember a single thing the physio therapist told me - gives me a photocopy of exercises and her work is done. CCAC is going to teach me - teach me or not I a cannot reach behind my back to change a dressing. I feel that the support staff both physio therapist & CCAC in the hospital do not want to actually assist the patients, but rather read from a binder, not touch the patient that way it is not their fault. They read their part of the chapter to you and their job is done - next. There are pieces that are put together to create the total health care package, but no one knows what the other one is doing or what is the flow of the process is. The nurse in the hospital told me that she sent the prescriptions to Shoppers - when Shoppers delivered it, not all the prescriptions were there. Another disconnect. I can't drive to the pharmacy to correct it so left as is.

input: My child was brought to Emerge with high blood glucose levels. As a result, he was admitted to ICU for one evening so that they could keep him under closer observation as he was in ketoacidosis. The following day, he was moved to the pediatric ward. In both areas the nurses and doctors that we dealt with provided excellent care, explaining what was happening and providing support. The nurses in the pediatric ward were particularly kind and supportive during a difficult time. The staff from the pediatric metabolic unit and the dietician were excellent and have gone above and beyond their duties. While in hospital they full explained everything and made sure that we were comfortable with the mechanics of providing insulin to our son and have continued doing so following our discharge. I can not thank XXXXX, XXXX and XXXXXXXX enough! All around, while we would prefer to not have to have a hospital stay or a diagnosis of Type I Diabetes for our child we couldn't have asked for better care from the staff that we dealt with.

input: As result of being discharge post spinal surgery with 50 % of pain meds as compared to during hospital stay my wife had me transported by ambulance to another hospital closer to home two nights in a row 'cause I was screaming in pain. They could not/would not transfer me back to XXX and ambulance also could not/would not deliver me there. They treated me in emerg dept for pain with IV drugs and discharged me. Ultimately my son drove me back XXX emerg dept where he advised clerk he had been in touch with surgeon's office (Dr XXXXXXX) and surgeon said he would meet me in XXX emerg dept at end of his day.. Dr couldn't find me 'cause apparently I had been registered under him, not as XXX patient. My wife called once to see what was happening and again she was told XXX did not have me registered. How the fuck was she to know I was registered under Dr's name. XXXXXXX came looking for me the next day and just by dumb luck I saw him, called him over and he he quickly arranged for an Xray which confirmed bone graft had not be damaged by my writhing in pain. He gave me Rx for same pain med dosage I had been receiving during last two days of hospital stay, my wife eventually found me, took me home and within one day I was comfortable enough to begin my proscribed physio light of short walk, sit, lie down, rest, repeat. With-in four days at home I was able to begin weaning off hydromorphone contin. Now approx 4 weeks post surgery I am nearly 80 % off narcotics and tylenol 325 mg is managing minor pain/discomfort. XXX discharged me with far too little initial pain meds and absolutely no info as to how to followup if needed. XXX emerg dept is so seriously over loaded that I felt the nurses (except for one angel) don't give a shit 'cause they don't have time. I feel the culture is to try to serve everyone fast and get them out even if the problem is not yet solved. It should not be up to the patient to get the attending surgeon to do an emerg followup, especially when the third un-introduced attending emerg Dr ordered an MRI (for which I was held overnight for and in fact was never done and not one nurse or Dr was able to tell when or even if it would ever be done, and it wasn't ) for an image of my back surgery when I have learned that an Xray is the preferred and definitive image for bone issues. Your left hand doesn't know what the right hand is doing. If I have anything to say about it, I will never again enter a XXXXXXXXXXXX. XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXX. I dare someone introduce themselves and contact me.

Thank you (please understand that the answers for admission and family should not be applicable answers)

input: I firstly visited the centre and all of the staff were exceptional. Once my test was complete, I was referred to emergency by the doctor and a male nurse escorted me to the ED in the freezing cold while they were wearing only scrubs and PPE, which went well above and beyond expected care.   I feel that the triage nurse in the ED could improve bedside manner and be mindful of privacy when talking to patients as they were very loud and expected patients to also speak loudly. In the waiting area you could hear all interactions with patients including their names and ailments. There were some inappropriate and insensitive comments made between triage and paramedics regarding a particular patient, and it seemed as though these staff members had no patience, were jaded, and were being a little rude. The patient was confined to a gurney and was very vocal about needing to go to the bathroom and being on the verge of an accident, and both triage and paramedics were dismissive and kept telling him to wait. It just seemed a bit inhumane and I wondered why they could not assist him right away (the two paramedics who bought the patient in were just standing around,) and I further wondered if the patient was being treated this way because they were clearly under the influence and from a vulnerable group. I wouldn't like to make assumptions but that's what I felt from my observations.   When I received triage I felt embarrassed that other patients could hear the interaction, which was uncomfortable having to disclose symptoms and existing medical conditions. It honestly left me with low expectations of the hospital and I initially thought about trying to leave.   However, once I was admitted, a nurse named XXXXX was amazing, patient, and very kind. XXXXX looked after me and made sure I was warm enough, as comfortable as I could be, and showed great empathy, sympathy, and compassion when conducting x-rays and taking blood. As did the doctor who also dealt with my care.   I appreciate the risk and stress involved treating patients during a pandemic and cannot

input: I understand that hospitals and our medical systems require more funding and that nurses and PSW's either work long too hours and/or do not always make a sustainable living for the duties they perform (many I'm sure, especially minorities, feel exploited) but many of the individuals that I encountered following my surgery and during my stay at XXXXXXXXX were unfriendly, bitter, and lacked social communication skills to make me feel confidence ie: my care. I understand that each person is unique and can either be introverted or extroverted, shy, tired, frustrated, etc. during their shifts, but given the profession they have chosen, many of the staff during my stay in the hospital lacked the basic social skills required for their job. I think this could be attributed to a lack of training and/or a personal bitterness that may be attributed to their working conditions, i.e., low pay, long hours, not enough hours to sustain a living, lack of respect from their supervisors and some patients, etc. Here are some situations I encountered with unfriendly, socially inept staff: I was asked to check in with admission on the day of my surgery at 5:30 a.m. When I arrived, 15 min. early, no one was in the cubicles in the admissions dept. As other patients started to arrive, the office and cubicles were still empty. Hospital staff did not arrive for work at admissions, until 6:45 a.m. (there was one female staff who arrived at 6 a.m. to set up, but she did not address me or the other patients ... simply ignored us. Of course, I and the other people waiting were stunned. When I was much younger and began my career, I learned that if I was work for late, I would be fired. What on earth is going on with punctuality today, especially in a hospital setting? As this was my second stay at XXXXXXXXX in a year (I had my first (XXXXXXXXX and then my second knee replacement XXXXXXXX), I did, however, find a 'great' improvement from my first stay in XXXXXXXXX. This time, nurses identified themselves upon entering the room, wore name tags and completed information on the white boards in my room. And all staff wore a top that identified them clearly from anyone off the street.. But the PSW's require way more training in greeting and taking care of the patients in a friendly and caring way, thus making the patients feel comfortable, safe, and cared for. There was (I think she may have been the PSW supervisor - middle age woman from the Philippines), during my stay who made me feel very uncomfortable and vulnerable. She was a bully, impatient, rude and abrasive each and every time she entered my room. And I overheard her treating her coworkers the same way. In fact, every PSW that attended with me was unfriendly and curt. And, the cleaning of the washrooms, which are shared with other patients, still needs a lot more work. The floor became filthy as did the toilet and sink. I was worried that I could easily catch a bug or infection from the lack of sterility and cleanliness. When it was time for me to leave upon discharge there was not one wheelchair to be found. My husband had to take the elevator and search throughout the hospital to find one in order to take me to the car. Not one staff person seemed to care and help. The search took close to one hour. However, on a more positive note, the entire staff of the Fracture Clinic, physicians, reception, etc. are most friendly, upbeat, and very, very helpful. The reason I chose XXXXXXXXX for my surgery is due to the excellent reputations and credentials of the physicians and specialists. They are world class and for this XXXXXXXXX can be proud. BUT there's still a lot of work to be done in training support staff within the hospital re: social skills and appropriate communication towards not only patients but coworkers as well. Again, I well understand the stresses and strains that these individuals are under in their jobs, especially working in a large city hospital in a cias diverse as XXXXXXX. But a smile, word of encouragement, explanation of procedures, and basic respect for each other and their coworkers can go a long way in helping patients feel better and less vulnerable when recovering from surgeries.

input: I went to emerge for chest pain that I had a feeling was a pulled muscle. I was going to just brush it off as that but my dad 2 days earlier had irregular heartbeat which maid me go there on the next day. All staff up to dr treated me as such an emergency. Sure, for stitches or broken bone that could heal itself you might spend some extra time there but not with my condition. I was overwhelmed at all the attention I was receiving and all the staff treated me with the utmost attention. I was very pleased after all this as with CAT scan and ultrasound found something on my liver. That was another scare but ended up being something that could have been there from when I was a child. But all the tests and scans were given to me in quick order. The stress test dr can kiss my a## though!!! His staff was great and punctual until they said wait for the doc to come give his results. Staff had me in and ready for him in 40 mins. I sat in the office walking up and down his hallway periodically. 35 mins I sat there for him to come into the office say hi look at my results and tell me my recovery time is remarkable. And as he walked out the door says quit smoking. 1 1/2 mins tops!!! But everything with my original condition for emergency visit up to stress doc was fantastic!!! Keep up the good work. I will not feel any anger to those taken ahead of me!!! Sincerely XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

I realize mistakes happen but 2 doctors and the radiologist missed it. I would definitely return to XXXXXXXXXX and I won't let this experience sour my perspective. Things can be missed especially with children.

input: The hospital experience was excellent. I felt like I was in good hands from start to end and it helped me to feel less afraid of my surgery. The doctors, nurses and staff were all kind and professional, except one nurse. The XX alarm button on the machine would go off at the slightest movement. I annoyed this nurse for that reason and the machine beeped the whole shift. No one explained to me how I was supposed to use the machine while I was aware. No one told me what was in it. No one told me how/how long I was to take the meds prescribed me after I left. But while at the hospital, when my pain level rose, the nurses did take care of me. To improve the experience, I would say that the whole medication information should be addressed after the patient is fully aware and before they leave, and possibly fix your drip machines so they aren't so sensitive! Beyond that, the stay there was excellent, truly. I felt I was in good hands before, during and after my surgery. And a special shout out to the volunteers, they were absolutely wonderful and so helpful!! And I'd take 20 annoyed nurses to be able to still say I had as successful a surgery as I had there, and feel so much better now! Thank you for taking care of me.

input: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX My day nursing staff was exemplary. There were so many professional facilitators available to me (physio, speech, mental health, etc). The surgeons, doctors, and interns were truly amazing and caring. My experience at University Hospital was a 10 out of 10. My sincere admiration and appreciation goes to the incredibly organization of the professionals ready to help me and I'm sure many other patients. I am currently dealing with Stage 3 lung cancer and was rushed to the hospital by ambulance because I suffered a seizure at home. I had a tumor on my brain. The incredibly Dr. XXXXXX operated and a day and a half later, I returned home - in time to watch the semi-final football match, leading to THE SUPER BOWL!!! It just doesn't get better than that. Thank all of you for saving my life. I'm doing well and my tumor is shrinking due to Dr. XXXXXXX's urgent appeal to start an immunotherapy drug that wasn't yet covered in XXXXXXX. The drug company sponsored me and there is great hope for me. I was the first person in Canada to use this drug for lung cancer. XXXXXXXXXXXXX

input: The nurses in day surgery were wonderful. My procedure consisted of 2 scopes. The medication given to relax me was NOT sufficient. I was awake the whole time but unable to speak due to a scope down my throat. Not only was this painful, but incredibly uncomfortable. I have had these scopes in the past and never experienced anything like this. In addition, watching the doctors remove items was extremely stressful and scary. I have to return in a week to have another procedure and am very worried about it. I should note that due to the pandemic no other family members were able to come into the hospital. Thank you for allowing me the opportunity to write about my experience.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

The nursing staff lacked compassion and interest. Overall it was not a good experience and I was fortunate to only have to stay two nights.

input: From attachment - I am writing this concerning the questionable actions of a Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.  My mother was admitted to XXXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, because she was extremely weak.  Her blood pressure upon arrival to the hospital was around 80/54 mmHg, her heart rate was over 1108PM, and her potassium level was 2.2.  The ER doctor told us she needed to be kept overnight for monitoring, and IV was started immediately.  She ended staying for six night and was discharged on XXXXXXXXXXX.  When Dr. XXXX spoke to us the day before her release he mentioned that her potassium concentration was 3.3, which was an improvement from the previous day (3.1).  However, he mentioned it was still too low.  He said that if the blood test taken the following morning revealed an improved potassium level, she would potentially be ready discharge.  The day of her release her potassium was 2.95 (a decrease from the previous).  She was also forced to take her oral pills in the presence of a nurse, who was there under the orders of the doctor.  My mother was incredibly insulted at the notion that she would lie about taking her medication.  She has no reason to want to stay in the hospital for any longer than absolutely necessary.  In fact, she has no reason to want to remain unhealthy for any longer than necessary.  To imply that her condition was not improving, because she was lying about taking her meds is incredibly disrespectful.  What I fail to understand is why she was released when she clearly had not reached full health.  Her potassium concentration was lower than what it was the previous day, her diarrhea was not improving, and her diastolic pressure was still indicating hypotension.  She was also taking her medication so the fact that her health was not improving was not intentional.  She ended up being admitted to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXX and ended up staying for ten nights.  What is most disappointing is that the doctors at XXXXXXXXXX tried to locate the source of the issue (enterocolitis) while the doctors at XXXXXXXXX simply kept prescribing potassium chloride and anti diarrhea medication.  It is very unfortunate that XXXXXXXXX does not provide the appropriate care that their patients need.  For the foreseeable future we will not be admitted to XXXXXXXXX even in the case of an emergency as we are not confident in doctors.

Hospital lacks beds - patients rested on stretchers  4. Overall nurses are overwhelmed and have difficulties coping with emergency patients added to the hallways,  Yours truly spent 4 days on a stretcher in this ward, would have preferred to remain in the emergency area

input: Following my check - in, I went to the bathroom and, on leaving, I stopped at the nursing station to ask for a drink of water.  I was completely ignored by both the doctors and nurses.  I said 'excuse me', and one doctor looked up and I asked for some water.  He asked what I was in for - I told him and he said I would be brought some water.  I waited an hour - no water.  I then pressed the button on the bed and 30 minutes later a nurse came and then brought me some water.  The other major problem was the continual 'social' noise from the nursing station which could be heard all through the XXXXXX Dept.  Very disturbing/distracting for patience!  I believe that the 'social activity' in the Nurses Station could delay XXXXXXXXX treatment by up to 30 percent.  Finally, the doctor told me I had nothing wrong. when my family doctor, Dr. XXX told me that I did, indeed have an attack of diverticulitis.

input: When I was brought into to XXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX I was in critical condition no one thought I was going to make it through the night. No one told my wife anything. No one introduced themselves to my wife or told her anything. My wife was there and they let her stay longer than the normal visiting hours. They told me the next day that they let her stay because they didn't think I was going to make it through the night and they did not want to kick her out. My wife had no idea they didn't tell her that. It was disgusting and disgraceful. They told her nothing. They told me some stuff but I was so high on drugs and painkillers that I didn't even recognize it that much. That's the only complaint I have against that hospital.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: Re XXXXXXX - abdominal pain. Arrived at hospital a bit after 1 pm. Only patient in waiting room. Others arrived later. Had blood work & taken to exam room at 2:45. Told blood work back & dr would see me soon. At 4:30 I went to desk. Asked if I'd been forgotten. Others had already seen dr & left. Told dr would see me shortly. At 5:45 I went to desk & told nurse I was going home, obvious that nothing serious or dr would have seen me. She took me back to exam room and dr saw me within 10 min. CT scan done - acute appendicitis. Surgery done that evening. I questioned why it was so long before I saw dr. Others that came in after me were seen & left while I still waited. She said they get a lot of patients with abdominal pain. It's something that can wait. Note re XXXXXXXX - internal infection. I was treated very promptly & professionally

Overall, I was very dissatisfied with my experience and had I not seen another professional I would have purchased a brace that would have in fact caused more harm to my injury.

input: I am a XX who has worked @ XXX for XX years. This was my second knee replacement so I knew what to expect. I had asked for pain meds on a few occasions and it was never brought promptly. The night of surgery I was made to wait 90 minutes to the point that I was in extreme pain. I was assisted once by physio to get up and walk. After that I was never offered assistance and was never checked up on when I got out of bed. My pre op nurses who prepared me for surgery were phenomenal. My OR nurses were kind & caring. And my PACU nurses went above & beyond to take excellent care of me. Every physician I encountered were excellent. My anesthetist, Dr. XXXX was exceptional in explaining everything in detail even though he knew I was an XX, and I actually work with him on a regular basis. Dr. XXXXXXXXX as always was amazing. There were a few other things that happened during my stay that surprised me as a fellow XXXXX I have had many surgeries and all four of my children were born at XXX and I have always had an amazing experience. So I was somewhat surprised this time. I am happy to speak to anyone else about this if needed. Thank you XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

input: I have contacted a lawyer to pursue legal action against XXXX for medical neglect. I entered the hospital with fewer problems than I left with due to the care I received. My chronic conditions were never addressed or managed. As a result of the lack of care I have had several serious infections and bed sores. I am bedridden now and the quality of my life has declined from my stay in hospital. Further, my physician (Dr. XXXXXXX - Team 3 4th floor Internal Medicine) never came to speak with me or my family about my condition, treatment or ongoing care. The surgeon consulted on my case sent his resident to answer whatever questions he could. Never was the indication of surgery discussed or explained. When my son demanded to speak with someone to get answers for my wife and family, all that was sent was a resident. When issues related to DNR were addressed, it was a 4th year clerk who came to speak to the family and myself. My opinion is that, unless you are a donor you are not important to physicians at XXXX. In addition to the horrible medical treatment, I was harassed three times to participate in a research study on 'quality of care'. The third attempt occurred when I was septic and unaware of my surroundings. My view of this hospital has changed dramatically as a result of my experience. As a proud UWO alum and life-long XXXXXXXX I was under the impression that our hospitals were high quality. My views now could not counter to this.
