input: When I went into emerg was thinking that it was because I had a fever because I had a kidney stint I told the surgeon that I take 2 drugs that compromise my immune system-he shrugged me off - he was basically saying that he wasn't going to give me an antibiotic - yet he said that I have infection in both of my kidneys-part way through my second night my fever shot right back up I was thinking that I would just get some antibiotics but I was admitted I ended up going from 2 in the afternoon until 2 in the morning without my meds - I told the drs I could go into shock without it and I'm in agony I was ready to scream and I was ready to go out of my mind I told Dr Xxxxx (sp??) that I needed my meds and he said that he would take care of it SOON this was at 2:30 in the morning - I kept asking the nurse until 6 in the morning but I didn't get anything so at 6 in the morning I finally got one oxycodone pill 50 mg less than what I normally take told the dr at 6 am that he was a liar before he even got the chance to speak - he told me that I would get my meds SOON not 6 or 8 hrs later - I didn't want anything more to do with Dr XXXXXX so Dr XXXXX took over and told me that I would likely get my meds around 8 or 9 am so at that point I was told that I would have to wait yet another couple of hours for my meds so I said that I'd had enough and I signed myself out-I went home and took my meds that I was supposed to take and laid down-I am still so mad about the pain that I had to go through especially when I was at the hospital and especially when I could've gone into shock- the one thing I want to stress is that it was out right ridiculous that they told me that the pharmacy was closed-also the dr telling me that I would get my meds SOON when it was like more than 16 hrs to me that's not soon. It was so stupid. The nurses were great other than the drs they were all great. I wouldn't give Dr. XXXXXX the job of shoveling out a horse stall.

input: I was very disappointed with the care I received at XXXXXXXXXXXX.  Although I have nothing but great things to say about XXXXXXXXXX and his surgical team, the care I received as an in patient was unacceptable.  My biggest complaint (I have a few) was the pain management protocol. I was taken off the pump the morning of my discharge, and left the hospital with my pain level at an 8.  I was unable to bend my knee to sit in the wheelchair (I had a total knee replacement two days earlier).  I was obviously in distress as it took three nurses to try to get I the chair.  I had an hour drive home and the nurse told my husband to lay in the back seat.  The pain I felt on that drive home was unbearable as was my pain level for the next week or so.  I feel that this has slowed down my healing process.  Is there not a pain management protocol wherein patients have to have their pain controlled before discharge?  This is especially important with a knee replacement as you have to push through pain during Physio. End of my rant....

input: My mother is a XX year old woman.  I had to call an ambulance 3 times in 1 week was sent home where she should have been admitted in the first place nurse lied to paramedic and told them that we wanted to go home which was not true.  We had to pay $135.00 ambulance bill because of this error not to mention my mother could have died.  Had an other bad experience when my mother fell down a flight of stairs and broke her shoulder.  The doctor confirmed her shoulder was broken and said that there was nothing that they could do and they were sending her home at the time my mother was not living with me she was along.  I explained to the doctor that she was on Coumadin and that I was dealing with cancer and could not care for her and that my sister lived north of XXXXXXXXXX and could not help me out.  The doctor's response to me was "This is not a babysitting service."  She was sent home.  The very next day my mother started to hallucinate, apprehensive to call the ambulance because we knew that she would be taken to XXXXXXXXXX we called anyway.  My sister who came from up north told the attending doctor was he told me the day before and said, "She probably needs blood, is dehydrated, and probably has a UTI."  The doctor replied, "Are you a doctor?"  My sister responded by saying, "No I know my mother."  That day she needed 2 lt of blood, severely dehydrated and had a UTI infection.  There needs to be more care and compassion in your emerge department so when asked would I recommend XXXXXXXXXX?  Not too sure that I would, but unfortunately when we call an ambulance this is where we are always redirected.

input: As I said, they should have checked on me during the 2 1/2 hours in waiting room I didn't appreciate to be told to hurry up by nurse just before going into surgery. I was in extreme pain. Her words were "Hurry up Doctor is waiting" ... ??? I almost passed out twice and felt very nauseous I was sitting in chair as I was not comfortable to lay in bed They said I should have pressed the alarm button It was not near the chair that I was sitting in I was extremely weak and in a lot of pain When doctor finally came in he said I hear you have a sore tummy I believe the only reason he came after 2 1/2 hours is because my husband was in waiting room and greeter person asked if she could help him That she noticed he had been waiting quite awhile He said my wife has been waiting over 2 hours to see a doctor The young girl immediately went to get information for my husband and I believe that's the only reason the doctor finally came to check on me The hospital was not busy at the time I entered and no one checked on me I knew it was my appendix After doctor came to see me, the procedure went quickly at that point once they realized I was quite sick I am thankful that there was a surgeon that night. Not sure what would've happened if she was not there Thank you XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

input: From attachment - XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Mrs. XXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXX Executive Vice President Patient services + chief practice officer XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX  Dear XXXXXXXXXX, Please see attached two pages that explains my very bad experience at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Emergency department.  Regards. XXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX  I had a very bad experience at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX emergency department.  I had a dull ache which appeared around belly button and under my breast bone.  My pain was gradually becoming worse, as if I was having contractions, and started vomiting.  I was taken to the hospital by ambulance, and the pain was unbearable.  They took blood and after hours of wailing Dr. XXXXX came in and told me it's virus and if the pain doesn't go away to come back in 2 days.  I asked him why he is not doing xray or other tests, he told me it's not necessary.  They put IV medication but the pain was still there, so they gave me morphine, prescribed me pain killers and sent me home.  The same pain continued, and after 2 days took me back to the hospital, and another doctor looked after me, they did CT scan and was told my appendix has ruptured, and they need to operate, but since there was other emergencies my operation was delayed more than 27 hours. the doctor came in and explained that it's too late to operate now, because they are all tired and also it's dangerous because so much time has passed, that the infection has spread to my other organs.  After 3 days of stay at the hospital they sent me home I was in so much pain that after staying home for one day, my friend took me to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX where they did CT scan, blood test and put a catheter.  They gave me antibiotics and painkillers through IV, and after a week they sent me home with a catheter where a nurse came every day to flush the catheter.  After 4 weeks I had another CT scan, and then they took the catheter out. was told I will be operated in XXXXXXXX to have my ruptured appendix out, because it's not safe to do it earlier.  In conclusion because of the long emergency wait at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and misdiagnosis of Dr. XXXXX I suffered so much and still have to go through operation.

input: I had to go back to the triage desk and ask them to get me something for pain for my kidney stone attack. I have numerous drug allergies and had to list them over and over again to all the different nurses and doctors I encountered. Emergency urologist gave me a prescription for a drug I was allergic to despite all this and swiftly left. I had to wait longer to leave because they had to find another doctor to change the prescription. Thank goodness I can read! Once I finally was given something for pain, I was left to sit in a straight waiting room chair in the hallway. NOBODY checked to see if I was ok, nor did they keep me informed of my status. I was invisible to them, though I was sitting across from the nursing station. I was never asked about my mother tongue (french). Though my answers to the survey questions seem satisfactory, my experience was not pleasant. Unless I am in a life and death situation, I do not want to go through this ER.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh
input: When I first checked in at the ER, the male nurse at the station made a comment to me that I've been to the ER a lot lately. I didn't appreciate his comment and was actually surprised he would say that. What business is it of his if I go every day to the ER? I really wish I had said something to him at that time or at least put in a complaint about him. My visit to the ER on this day was unrelated to the first two visits (sore knee). I was at the optometrist for a check up and she found something on my eye that she wanted checked right away. She advised me to go to the emergency department because she thought it would be faster then trying to get an appointment with an opthalmologist The one problem about going to the ER was that there wasn't an opthalmologist on call that afternoon. I ended up getting an appointment at their office the next day. I was actually surprised that an opthalmologist wasn't available.

input: I had an emergency c-section. My answers above responded directly to the questions, however wanted to let you know that the only place I felt that the care was lacking was in explaining the physical rehab from this surgery. This is a major and traumatizing surgery for a new mother, I would have liked to have had a discussion with the OB or physician as part of my care before discharge.

Thank you! I am extremely grateful for the opportunity to share my experience Good luck! My objection to application of vaseline (unreadable) bandaging was because they are petroleum based, surely, traditional medicine can realize that moisture is not the only preferred condition to consider - like healing as well! It was actually more than a week before the (unreadable) got to see my leg! Errors were made in using a topical cream that clearly stated on the label not to use on sensitive areas Something, I only saw after it had been applied very liberally all over my foot + leg. This resulted in waking me in the middle of the night with burning fire. With only two nurses on staff at night, I very willingly removed the bandage + thoroughly washed off the cream with saline solution + simply, that the nurse hang a clean towel to wrap my leg in until morning. I finally turned to holistic remedies, including coconut oil (antibacterial, antiviral + antifungal) to heal the resulting inflammation + seizing of the muscles of my left foot + leg due to (unreadable), during a period of slightly more than a year P.S. I am prompted to, honestly + without prejudice, share that the protocol of the physiotherapy dept at XXXXXXXXXXX that was applied to me as to give me the absolute + unquestionable sense of being "kicked out" of the hospital. All the extreme pain I experienced during this condition left me extremely vulnerable and contrary to my normal sense of strength, independence, respect and gratitude for all I receive + experience in my life. I am deeply grateful to all the nurses + their devotion + talents to their calling that helped to ease the "push" + lack of empathy of even asking how I felt, considering my misguided expectations! XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX P.S. Now, well into my third week home, I slowly realized I was in a bit of a state of shock, having been discharged before I "had my legs under me"! I couldn't walk well enough at all! I have just discovered in 5pg list of exercises to do at home - why was I not told + given them while in rehab! My nurse, the day of my discharge actually had to run up to (unreadable) to get the folder, why I waited w/ W.T. outside the door! There is still light swelling - not sure what to do!

input: I ended up leaving the hospital on my own! I was treated so poorly that I was scared for my health! Nurses were rarely available and never changed my bedding . The nurses were sporadic in wearing COVID-19 protective equipment! The room I was in was directly across from the nurses station and I was so sleep deprived I rarely could cope! Packaging from medical procedures like I V changes were carelessly left on the floor! urinals were put on the same table as the food was served on. I never had proper pain management one doctor was wanting to reduce them one wanted to increase them! Bed was so uncomfortable I had bed sores when I left the hospital. One evening I went into my bathroom and there was a man masturbating and when I complained to the nurse he told me I should knock I was furious I didn't know the bathroom was shared I felt very unsafe! I left on my own I was unable to walk and upon leaving the security guard was literally grabbing the wheelchair from me! The lady who was the supervisor of my floor spoke such poor English I couldn't understand her and when I mentioned that she became very aggravated! XXXXXXXXXXX is geared to older geriatric care I certainly felt the hospital was not geared towards people like myself .

input: During my hospital stay the nurses were so kind and helpful answering questions and concerns. Prior to hospitalization my questions and concerns were addressed by Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXX and post-surgery Both myself and family felt unheard We realize all are very busy and rushed but concerns should have been addressed I know my body and knew something was wrong and was discounted (infection was suspected) Told that "it was post op healing" My nurse listened to our concerns and checked vitals and realized something was definitely wrong She called the GI team for Dr. XXXXXXXXX After a couple of hours and a few calls - one directly to Dr. XXXXXXXXX team members came to see me. Thank goodness for my nurses persistence I had abscesses and had three drainage tubes placed inside me what was supposed to be a one to four day stay ended up being a two and half week stay On the day of discharge I was assured all paperwork was in discharge package - as well all info had be sent for home care That was not the case No appropriate papers were sent Since my stay in XXXXXXXX at hospital continue to receive daily nursing care - and had to go to emergency and was admitted in XXXXXXXX and again treated for another abscess. It is felt that if my concerns had been addressed earlier the outcome would have been different

input: I was having trouble seeing & trouble walking. Upon arrival a hospital guy insisted that I would sit in chair in waiting room for the 6=7 hours this would take. I have terrible back pain & 2 injured knees that cause pain sitting, he said that it was like a doctor's office that I had to sit in a chair. I said my husband was coming in car & would arrive soon & that he would take me home then because I was unable to get off ambulance stretcher & sit in chair. I offered to lay on floor, I also offered to wait in car when husband arrived because seat goes back. He said that we don't do that here. The EMS guy luckily found me a lazy boy chair that went flat and transferred me to that and I was laying in waiting room surrounded by the other sick people. The doors to outside kept opening & closing & freezing me. I was taken to the in & out treatment room after many hours. The doctor insisted that he would only concern himself with my eyes, ignore the rest of my problems. Eventually I got him to give me a trigger point injection & xray my back. Are we were really only allowed to have our eyes looked into when you have multiple problems. I certainly had 3 of 5 signs of stroke (vision, balance, headache). I was returned to laying down in waiting room then eventually the dr came into waiting room & told me as I lay there in a packed waiting room, that my case was complex and that he thought I had MS, but gave me no recommendation on how to follow up on this. He did not order a MRI to try to confirm or deny this diagnosis, he did not refer to me a neurologist, or have on call neurologist see me, which would have helped. Waiting room medicine is worse than hallway medicine. It is awful having dr come in full waiting & discuss your private medical matters there. If I had a stroke - the magic 4 hour window was gone before I was seen. There should be places to have private discussions with doctors.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: Well I'd just like to say that I had been there the day previous and when my wife and I went in there were 4 people waiting so I had thought that wed get in quite quickly. The day before I had been coughing up a lot of blood sometimes drowning in it. We got there early afternoon shortly after the room had filled with native people and by 6:30 at night the room had emptied. My wife went up and asked if we could have a place for me to lay down and the receptionist said you'll just have to wait your turn so I then informed her I was going home to lay down. So then the next morning we arrived early and I was taken into a room immediately and sat there for I think an hour and 15 minutes in this little room where renovations were going on. Then a nurse came to talk to me and ask me questions then they came back and informed me I was going to have an x ray. The x ray department was incredible. They sent me back to the room and then everyone that was helping me starting wearing masks and they brought me a mask. Then the Doctor came in and in a nutshell this is what she told me I'm going to give you antibiotics which I was already on but she changed them to what she thought would be more acceptable. She basically said I don't know why you came to see me even though I was coughing up blood. Then when Doctor XXXXXXX came back a few days later he was furious. He saw my condition and that I was coughing up blood and he said the emergency should have ordered a ct to see why I was bleeding so much. Now I did have a ct and that department was absolutely awesome. Previous to this my sister and brother who are both younger than I both passed away of cancer and their treatment at XXXXXX was wonderful they did an amazing job. In regard to the doctor that asked me why I came to see her I am now being treated for lung cancer so she missed the boat on that one.

input: Overall the hospital stay was okay. Not sure how often linens are changed but I had to ask for linen and changed my bedding myself. My roommate often needed assistance and often looked to me for help. She did not have access to her call bell and asked me to press mine. After pressing a few times a nurse finally came to my area swinging the curtain back and stood there like I was bothering her. I explained it was my neighbour that needed help and I was only calling because she could not reach her call bell. The other thing I found disturbing was waking up to a bad smell. There was feces on the floor at the foot of my bed. The nurses had just finished cleaning up my roommate after having a bowel movement but left feces on the floor. Hospitals are supposed to be clean and place where people go to heal. Carelessness like this puts patients at risk of contracting infectious diseases. I had to ask my Doctor for permission to leave the hospital earlier than intended as I felt I would recover better at home. I remember one nurse, her name is XXX, she was amazing. input: Some questions I was unable to answer for you questionnaire as I was not discharged from ED I was admitted to hospital for 8 days following for a lengthy horrific stay!  I wish you questionnaire covered all of that because that would give you the honest scoop on how your hospital is ACTUALLY fairing.  Most the nurses in ED were friendly, volunteers were friendly!  The doctors were upfront and knowledgeable.  The fact you have a bunch of ill patients stuffed in chairs on narcotics and walking around from pod to pod for assessments is another story and a dangerous one, but that's my two cents!  I didn't feel comfortable being given different pain medications and then asked to walk around to see doctors in 'privacy' for updates in curtained off rooms!  There's no such thing as patient privacy with monitors with our names everywhere and people's charts laying on tables and names being over head paged when they want you back in pod 16.  It is an awful set up.  The nurses are over worked in that Internal Waiting room.. so many patients and one nurse just shuffling them all around hoping for a pod chair to clear out to stuff the next sick person into.  Then if you're lucky enough to get admitted like I was and get a stretcher in yellow zone, you can lay there and smash your already sore head off a box on the wall because there was zero spacing between the stretcher and this gauge thing on the wall and there won't be a call bell or anything to be able to reach a nurse if you need one, so good luck to you!  Super wowing experience I had in your ED!  That was just the first of many wowing experiences I had at XXXXXXXXX!  Enjoy your boxed lunch in there if you're lucky enough to find one, I really hope you're not taking any medication that requires you to eat before taking them.  Not that any of the nurses actually cared about that anyway.  The best one was when your doctor specifically orders you some meds for pain and something for anxiety to help you rest because you've been in pain and sitting for countless hours in a chair but your nurse is obviously smarter than that doctor and says 'no we don't give those kinds of meds during the day, the first line of defense for a 'headache' is Tylenol' and refuses to give the ordered meds until I was transferred upstairs to the floor! leaving me in pain and awake!  That's is the type of treatment I received in your ED!  No.. I would NOT recommend anyone go there, nor would I go back there!  Quite disgusted by the care and compassion I received from your frontline staff in ED!

input: From attachment - I would like to bring to your attention, my experience, when I was admitted to the emergency department at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.  I arrived on XXXXXXXXXXXXX, .  With a bloody face, in shock, weak and scared, I was taken to the emergency department after registration, then waited for 3 hours.  The doctor told me I needed to get both an x-ray and CT scan done.  During the scan, the nurse, who saw my bloody face and the sand around my mouth from the fall, simply handed me a Kleenex.  Rather than try to assist me and clean me up, apparently, I was expected to do that on my won, in the state I was in.  I was appalled at the commend she made, "you must have been embarrassed about falling down."  At XX years old, I was more concerned with the extent of my injuries, worried about the possibility of any broken bones.  The last thing I would feel is embarrassment!  As it turned out, I broke my nose, needed stitches, and ended up with a concussion.  Such a comment, does not reflect well for a medical professional's bed-side manners!  Other than the above disappointment, I must say, the emergency doctor who attended to me, showed great concern and compassion, and took good care of me.  He stitched me up and said a nurse would come by and clean me up.  No such nurse came by to clean me up.  Next, I was just told to go home.

input: The emerg Dr misdiagnosed me, interpreting old fractures in the x-rays of my wrist as ones sustained that day. What he communicated to me was exactly what turned up in CT scans from my accident in XXXX (this was determined after a phone consult with my family Dr). I was put in a cast for nothing. At my second fracture clinic appointment, Dr XXXXX told me there were no obvious displaced fractures in my wrist. When I asked Dr XXXXX if I should be using a brace or support for my badly sprained ankle, he asked if I had been given a brace or boot at emerg, and he seemed shocked or surprised that I hadn't been given any such device. He got me an ankle brace right away. The crutches I had been given at emerg were ill fitted. An occupational therapist observed this when he came for an assessment. At my next fracture clinic, someone was kind enough to adjust a crutch for me (I was only using one at that point). The x-ray technician was a bit clueless. He accidentally bumped my injury, and instead of saying sorry or asking me if I was ok when I cried out, he asked 'what happened?' Note: two different practitioners saw me at my fracture clinic appointments, not sure which one was Dr XXXXX The second one is a huge Elvis fan (my service dog's name is XXXXX so we had a friendly chat about Elvis the musician). The second practitioner was the one who fixed my crutch. The volunteer at the emerg entrance was very helpful in getting me a wheelchair. One of the nurses got me a chit to take a taxi home. Someone else was kind enough to help me get to the bathroom. So it wasn't all bad, just angry about the misdiagnosis and ill fitting crutches, and annoyed with the x-ray technician. I still don't know/haven't been told what exactly was affected in my wrist.

input: There were some times when doctor's or people talking to me was very difficult to understand due to the masks and I had to listen very closely and had to have them repeat themselves occasionally.  PT's wife he received excellent nursing and the people I spoke to through ed and directed my call to the ICU were fantastic.  I phoned about 6 in the morning hoping to speak to the nurse I had spoken to previously.  She was excellent and very forth coming with information.  When I was directed to the nurse XXXXXX she was terrible.  I explained who I was and there was silence and I had to ask for an update.  I had to have her repeat some things as I had trouble hearing the terms she was using  which could have been caused my an accent or a mask.  She sounded annoyed by this clarification request.  There was no acknowledgement to me when I explained who I was.  It was dead silent and I was unsure what to ask but there was no initiative to provide information she was dismissive.  I knew I could call back and speak to another nurse  as there would be a shift change but this interaction prevented me from calling back.

input: I must emphasize that nurses were very attentive and caring during my stay. However on discharge, they did not lock the wheelchair and having had foot surgery I came very close to falling. This was not a good experience. The other point more important, is never did I see my surgeon after the surgery nor did he talk with my family member. At some point very early the next morning a male person appeared at my bedside, never identified himself, and I had to ask him who he was. Again I was not given a name just that he was part of Dr. XXXXXXX team. I was awoken from a sedated sleep, he did not give me an opportunity to wake up before asking me questions to which I did not respond very well. So he left and I never saw a doctor again, even on discharge. I was very disappointed in this incident about the doctor. But I must emphasize, other than the incident on discharge, the nurses were outstanding despite being rushed off their feet.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I was most pleased and very satisfied with the care which I received in the emergency department at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. I initially went to by physician's office. He was not in and the receptionist suggested I should go to the emergency department. The emergency department was not busy. I think there were only one or two other persons waiting. The nurse on duty in the department saw me right away and took much blood pressure was she completing the forms. She noticed an abnormal pulse and immediately took me to an examining room and had Dr. XXX see me. An excellent doctor who explained everything which he was doing and what he thought my problem was. He gave me an EGA and basically he and his assistants spent the rest of the afternoon monitoring my condition. They were most professional and caring in their help. I was not in pain but I felt weak and my condition had deteriorated over the past few weeks. My wife insisted that I had to do something and took me to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. Dr. XXX had Dr. XXX, an internist, check me and an appointment was made to see Dr. XXX.

input: Patients waiting for their first interaction with a doctor need reassurance from time to time that they have not been forgotten. When I completed the triage process I walked to the Emergency Department and placed my paperwork in the basket indicated. I had an ECG quickly and then sat back down in waiting area. It was two hours before somebody spoke to me again. I did feel that my paperwork was lost and I was forgotten. At a minimum, patients waiting should be acknowledged every 30 minutes and an expectation set for additional wait time. Most people have no issue waiting if an expectation has been set. Waiting knowing nothing about how long this will take is very unsettling.

I was truly disappointed in how this was not handled, not even considered to be an issue. input: Hospital visit was excellent in every way but one. One night (XXXXXXX I believe) I had a nurse that was terrible. I will keep details short. Her name was XXXX, she came on duty at 7 pm. I told her I needed water, hadn't had my glass filled since 4 pm. She never brought me water until 10 PM (I was able to flag down an housekeeper for water at 8 PM. Short after 10 pm I told XXXX I needed a pain pill, she never asked my degree of pain (it was 8) and came back with Tylenol 2. I said she might just well give me a baby aspirin. I said can you give me morphine. She went away and at 11 pm came back with two small pills. I asked what it was, she said ten times more powerful than Morphine. I said if that is true give it to me, I continued to be awake and extreme pain until 2 am (3 hours). I buzzed XXXX and asked for more, better pain pills. She said she had to wait until 3 am (4 hours between pain pills). I said okay but please be here at 3 am, the pain is unbearable. She didn't come at 3. I buzzed her a 3:08 am and said I need those pills. She showed up at 3:15 with the same two little pills that were of no use before. I said to her that those pills were useless at 11 pm,what makes you think they going to work at 3 am. Another nurse came in the room and I told I know I was allowed stronger pain killers, like morphine. She says do you want morphine, I said yes. She gave me a shot and within 3 minutes I had pain relief and went to sleep in about 10 minutes. Also whenever XXXX came in to take my vitals, she would leave my table, with my water pushed out of reach. I believe that this nurse could be a real danger to someone with life threatening problem.

Very upsetting - disconcerting - and not acceptable as standard of care.  I arrived at XXXXXXXXXX at approximately 9:00 pm on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX + was in emergency until 10:00 pm on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX whom I was moved to a holding area until about 12 midnight - when I was told that I would be moved to surgery "shortly" I went to the operating room around 12:30 am - and post recovery was moved back to an overflow room as a "temporary" move - awaiting another room - I was never moved from the overflow area + forced to stay there for my remaining time in hospital  The space was awful + inadequate.  Over crowded with 4 patients crammed into 1 room - with a very small curtain area that help my bed - barely  There was no privacy  The room was extremely loud + not conductive to recovery at all  The room had no washroom - we had to go far down the main (public) hallway - no call button - and was substandard in every way.  Far below any standard or acceptable hospital room for a Canadian hospital.

input: The breastfeeding facilitator in the class I attended should assist new mothers right after giving birth to assist with breastfeeding to begin with since she can resolve problems quickly if any and to get the best advice possible nurses are helpful but having someone who is an expert right off the bat can help significantly to start & continue breastfeeding if she had been the person to help me first I would not have had to give my newborn formula all I needed was a breast shield which she recommended at my appointment after discharge.  I insisted I had for 4 days and I could have breastfed exclusively throughout my stay instead of feeding my newborn with formula as suggested by my nurse  The lactation consultant at the post partum clinic visit new moms to assist solely on breastfeeding as this is their speciality this would greatly help new moms and could have helped me a lot.

input: I spent 15 hrs in the Emergency area of the hospital that day sitting on a chair in the hallway. I arrived in Emergency around 10 am and moved to an observation area for further assessment shortly after that. I sat in that area for 2 hrs before a doctor realized no one had come to even speak with me since I arrived. I was assessed and put through a series of tests which revealed a bowel blockage and was admitted shortly before 9 pm that evening. It wasn't until I begged a nurse at 1:00 am to check on my room arrangement that I was finally allowed to get into a bed. She was apologetic but admitted that she forgot to call a porter when the doctor signed the admission papers hours earlier. I can only imagine the effects that this pandemic has had on all front line workers and staff at hospitals but a little more care and double checking on things such as this would really help. Also, the conversations that nurses have among themselves really needs to be reserved for more private areas. I heard a lot of insulting, insensitive and sarcastic remarks made about doctors, nursing staff and ER patients in that observation area from the nurses on duty which should never be overheard by the public. Pandemic stress perhaps to blame but not acceptable behaviour at any time.

input: I am XXXX's Mom, she was the patient and I accompanied her to the ER, I was extremely disappointed as her Mom with the triage nurse, she was a very heavy set woman, she was quite rude. She made us feel like we were an inconvenience and a number. I have never seen my daughter so sick, she had a fever of over 102 that she had for 5 days, nothing I gave her would bring it down, she was very lethargic and had a terrible cough. It took 7 hrs to see a doctor which is completely unrealistic when you have a very sick individual. The doctor was amazing, and apologized for our long wait, he diagnosed her with influenza, a virus, and some sort of bronchitis or something in her chest, and said it would get better within a week.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: We did not like the nurse named XXXXXXX.  After a 30+ hour labour I was given a c-section. I found it to be so traumatic that I do not think that I want to try and have a second child in case I need to go through this horror again.

input: The doctors were very kind, helpful, and informative as were the nurses. That being said, I wish that there was a little bit more focus on learning to breastfeed while in hospital. I know that there are classes offered daily, but being as weak as I was from surgery and then hemorrhage, it would have been nice for a lactation consultant or other nurse to visit me to instruct me on proper technique and potential side effects of the medication I was on (i.e. 'sleepy baby'). Perhaps then my daughter wouldn't have lost so much weight in the initial days so quickly (higher than average).

input: I understand that aspects of my survey have very low scores. Let me elaborate on why that is. The time I spent in emergency was not longer than I expected, I think the pace I was moved at was reasonable. The time it took to be processed from one area to another created no problems for me. The information I received was accurate and helpful, and I am recovering well using the guidance given to me by staff. However, the person who performed my ultrasound was very rude to me when I attempted to ask questions about what results she was seeing. She also performed a vaginal ultrasound, which I found to be invasive and unnecessary. The person who performed the procedure reacted aggressively when I tried to make inquiries. It felt as if she was trying to shut me up and it made me feel dehumanized. My next issue was the lack of communication with my family once I was admitted to my surgery. My mother and sister attempted to access information about my surgery and could find no one to help them. They are still unaware of how long I spent in recovery, surgery, etc. They were left in the dark about the status of their loved one. Instead of looking for them in the waiting room, the doctor looked for them in my room. When she did not find them there, there was seemingly no further attempt to locate them and relay information to them by the staff. They made one attempt then immediately gave up. There was no attempt made to put my family's mind at ease while their loved one was having a surgery performed, and I believe that to be incredibly negligent. My final comment will be that I felt little support from staff when I was experiencing stress and pain. There was a point where I was in so much pain that I could not move, and when this was finally brought to a nurses attention, she didn't take my distress seriously and told me to 'stop crying.' This was probably 8 hours after my surgery. I understand that crying is not the most productive way of dealing with a situation, but it is also a natural human emotive response. I was made to feel hysterical after I had an organ removed from my body. It really seemed like she was trying to serve her own desire to not hear me crying rather than help me be in less pain. It really seemed like through a lot of my stay at the hospital that no one at all cared about my well-being, which made the experience of having surgery for the first time somewhat traumatizing. I felt like I was an object on an assembly line rather than a human being. Even as I climbed onto the table in which my surgery was being performed, the doctors were quick to remind me about getting my healthcard renewed as soon as I could to avoid fees. I can't think of a less appropriate time to bring up money than when a patient is minutes away from being cut open. In the future, I will be going to a different hospital in order to seek treatment. I have been admitted to hospitals in the past and have never had an experience that has affected me this way. I am not trying to disparage the hospital for personal reasons, I am simply being honest about my experience.

input: 40. Should be Blank. I received great care. Great surgeon and his team. Nurses gave great care. There was an issue with admission process. They system billing benefits was not explain at the pre op. Why not do this during pre op. Advised that there would be a bill for $1500 bill it was rectify after the fact. They are talking about the ward and semi private and I am 30 min before major surgery for spinal cord and neck surgery. Should have done at pre op a week ago not 30 minutes before. That really created dilemma. The care and surgery was great cannot put it in words. There was lots of people who dealt with me and they were great. The Anesthesiologist was awesome. Once rolled me through the doors I felt great. So totally contrast to the ED. The surgeons worked well together. I was nervous but now when I have to go back I will not be as nervous. I did not know what happen during the operation my surgeon and my staff were superb but I had to ask questions instead of them giving fluid information and that is hard after surgery and you are on medication. The ED and Triage is a mess space issue no reflection on the care. Front end north end. No good Security. Don't feel comfortable there. Property lines and no smoking signs. As a patient going for care and no place for smokers and it caused some stress. But you know Doctors and nurses have their spot. I was there for a week and had to go off property that caused a problem. The space issue not quality of care needs work. Triage and ED there for 8-10 working in the back were very rude. They don't know anything about me and they treated me very unprofessional. But when you have the uniform. I treated very well in the hospital. XXXXXXXX better than XXXXX. I received poor service no communication in the ED. I get they are busy and lots volume. My opinion they need to work on. There was a Crown Prosecutor and they did not treat her professionally either. Which is disappointing because the hospital is great. At the end of the day it needs to be address. The time before I had an issue with my leg but no communication about take the brace. Could have been dealt with better. I knew there was smaller braces and I cannot not use it. Waste of $60. they gave me menu and asked what I wanted to have.

input: I have to say that it is unacceptable to stay from 1 pm to 9 pm in recovery waiting for a room, no food, not allowed to use the washroom (had to use a bedpan when I could walk), constantly not getting any explanation as to why it took 8 hours to get a bed at 9 pm then I get to a room that has no bathroom door and no food at all. The nurse manager had to call down to get me a tray and it came an hour before lunch was served. The food is just disgusting. There is no need for hospital food to be cold when it is a hot meal and it stays sitting for so long that pasta gets stuck and mushy. Please look to other hospitals like XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX where the food is so much better. Even XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX's food is awful ... you must use the same services. I have to say my surgery went well and the doctors were great but the miscommunication between the floor and recovery needs to change. No patient should have to stay so long in a bed and not move ... have to say I have better hospital stays.

input: Admission was smooth. I was scheduled for an induction, and labor progressed far more rapidly than anyone anticipated. I had simply received cervical ripening gel, was monitored for one hour then told this would likely be a long process. Regular and increasingly painful unmonitored contractions ensued shortly thereafter and I requested nursing assistance three times. I assume my nurse was either busy or on break, because other nurses, who all three times came in at least 20 minutes after calling them, offered little care and compassion. It was obvious they felt I was overreacting, and on top of it failed to inform my nurse I needed assistance. One went so far as to suggest I cover up when the anesthesiologist comes in as I was topless on my bed sweating from labor pains. I asked her to call the anesthesiologist as I wanted the epidural immediately, which was my wish expressed upon admission, however this was not done. I laboured on my own for over two hours with zero monitoring, analgesia or assistance from staff. This was my first birth, and to experience it like this was frightening and disappointing at such an establishment. When my nurse arrived after two hours, she was shocked to find me 10 cm dilated and in transition. She had not been informed by the other staff of my condition or my requests. She quickly organized prompt care. She, several new nurses, the OB's, the anesthesiologist immediately all rose to the occasion at this point. A healthy baby was born 30 minutes later and I am grateful for that. I am disappointed that the nursing staff whose assistance I greatly needed carried an attitude of 'you're not my patient or responsibility', and assumed I was overreacting and therefore undeserving of care. This was a failure to meet the standard of care. They did apologize after the fact, which was appreciated. All staff in recovery were wonderful.

input: I found the lactation consultant in the Maternity Ward of XXXXXXXXX to be quite condescending, judgemental and lacking in compassion/ humanity. I did not find her helpful and am actually a little traumatized by my experience with her. She was the only part of my hospital stay that I did not care for at all. She seemed to be very technical and knew about the mechanics of breastfeeding but she was not understanding/considerate of the circumstances in which she is trying to relay this information. The women in the maternity ward (myself included) just gave birth and are sleep deprived. We are emotional, hormonal, exhausted. When speaking to new mothers, it would be nice for the lactation consultant to understand our situation and speak to us with dignity and respect as many of us are just tying to learn how to breastfeed for the first time in our lives. That lactation consultant is more suited to running a seminar but should not be allowed to interact directly with patients, especially new mothers.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I would have given XXXXXXXXX a perfect review, as I have in the past but this experience was not a good one.  Upon arriving at the ER I informed the nurse who registered us that my daughter has reflux and she had just spit up.  The nurse gave me a red slip and said we have to be treated with caution for covid because of her spit up.  I explained again and she said we have no option.  She sent us to the left of the waiting area.  I've always been placed in a separate room, isolated from others, except this time.  When the 1st nurse arrived to look at my daughter she was familiar.  She had helped us the previous week and we were following up based on her symptoms.   The nurse asked why we were on that side and I told her I was nervous because the child across from us was vomiting and his father had the curtain open and mask down.  The child's father said he hoped his son didn't have covid.  The nurse was understanding and said she will try to put us in a room.  This never happened.   2 days after leaving XXXXXXXXX I started feeling sick and later both my daughter and I tested positive for covid.  We had not visited any other place. We all were negative the week prior when we did a routine check while at the hospital.   I have an immune compromised mother in my home and I suffer from severe asthma.  I obviously cannot say 100% that I contracted this from my visit to XXXXXXXXX but it's the only possibility.   The 1st nurse registering us should never had sent us there just because my daughter's reflux caused minimal spit up when we arrived. She didn't listen to my explanation or concerned.  I cannot say 100% we contracted covid from this visit but it's the only place we've been. Public health nurses who called for contact tracing also advised it's a great possibility that we contracted it at XXXXXXXXX. I'm very disappointed.  My baby went in for a hit on the head and came out with covid.  My entire household is now suffering because of negligence

input: I only had a 1 - 3 hour visit because of covid and no one going there, otherwise the wait is much longer than that at this ER.  I did not see the doctor or physician assistant WASH their hands before servicing me which is concerning during normal times let alone now in covid times.  Also, I need the doctor or physician assistant to be able to use a slit machine.  Both saw me and both were baffled by this machine that is essential to a diagnosis for herpes keratitis.  The sooner this is treated the less damage to my eye.  I've had it before and when I can't get into the ophthalmologist I'm forced to go to the ER for a referral.  I was very upfront about needing a referral for the ophthalmologist especially since neither could use the slit machine.  If they don't know how to use something, then just do a referral.  I feel like I should not have to wait for 2 hours just to get a referral.  Also, the doctor made it clear that he was not from my city, didn't understand how things 'worked' there, and that he was a family doctor so he wasn't up on the ins and outs of a slit machine. While I appreciated his truthfulness, and I could easily see he didn't know what he was doing, it did not instill confidence at the time.  Even when he said he was doing a referral I didn't feel confident that that was going to happen because he readily admitted he didn't know how anything worked at that hospital.  In fact, the next day when I had not heard from an ophthalmologist by noon, I was on my way to go back to ER to find out about my referral and if he had actually done it.  I literally had my shoes on and keys in hand on my way back to ER to see if the referral was done, when the ophthalmologist finally called.

input: I needed to come back for some testing because my newborn showed high levels for jaundice. Coming back to the hospital was horrible, we were told to come back to the same desk we left and they needed to draw her blood because it was still a high level. There is no room for this so we sat beside the elevators ... seriously while a nurse took her blood. Then had to wait for an hour and maybe see a doctor or maybe not. In the end she was okay but I didn't feel this was professional at all. Other than this our labor stay was incredible, Our nurse XXXXX was incredible, when our daughters heartbeat dropped she was calm focused and knew what she needed to do. Our Doctor seemed very uncomfortable from the get go, she needed to bring in Dr XXXX and then Dr XXXXXX, we had some serious complications. Dr XXXXXX was also calm, and explained everything. In the end our daughter was born healthy but the team was prepared. I couldn't thank them enough. Each nurse that came in to give XXXXX a break was wonderful as well.

On each of my first three visits i waited 4 hours each time as I watched people with sore ankles/knees come in an hour after me and leave an hour before me. 'it's up to your groin?', asked the Dr. - no longer being cellulitis, but the next thing up. He apologized and said yes. After that interaction my visits were quicker, but still a couple of hours each. I also had to ask one nurse to put on gloves before he hooked me up with the drugs - all during Covid no less. input: I was brought in with restraints. Insulin was pumped into me. The ward physician was useless. The psychiatrist was narrow minded. Someone allowed my XX yr old nephew to decide to have my license removed. The food was revolting. The regular physicians thought it would be a good time to treat my diabetes. I went through a lot of falls - my back was hurt and no one gave a damn. NRC HEALTH. Should you want examples of the crap that I had to go through whist a patient at XXXXXXXX I would feel happy to meet and discuss the treatment. I was brought in by ambulance and placed in restraints by 4 people for one old lady. During the falling down section, the aides would maneuver my body so my head was smashed against the door. Because I am a smoker and had pneumonia and pleurisy there was a great kerfuffle about my resistance to quit smoking and lose weight. The people on the ward that were drawing blood had my arms from wrist to shoulder covered in bruises. The doctors were listening to my XX year old nephew and decided to cancel my license. It took a family doctor and my real psychiatrist to rectify this situation. I am still very angry about this. The list of drugs that was in my handbag; the drugs were changed, insulin was administered, the meal plan was for a diabetic regardless of my wishes. Should anyone ever recommend that I go back to that damn hospital even for tests, I will refuse and would rather die at home than have that gang of incompetents treat me. This was my second go around with pneumonia, in XXXX I had a much worse case that XXXXXXXXXX took care of - even though I was in intensive care for a couple weeks at least they switched me over to cortisone products so I had a chance to fight the infection. During this stay I asked why they couldn't switch and was told not to bother.

input: I have NEVER had a hospital experience like I did at XXXXXXXXXXXXX. It wasn't perfect and there is always room to learn and grow (more so in terms of the system than in the people and experience), but all and all my heart was truly warmed by the treatment I received. There was a true abundance of compassion and conversation (the right balance of support, answering questions and explaining) and never once did I feel judged, ignored or mistreated by a doctor. I know now that I have a really complicated and newly researched disorder, but it was really hard to go through 3 1/2 years with no explanation and to be treated the way I was. I've been to so many emergency rooms (depending on where I lived or what family I was visiting) and specialists trying to get to the bottom of this or because I was flaring so severely that I was worried I was going to die. I've been laughed at, scolded, insulted, judged and so much more. I refuse to dwell in the past, instead, I am grateful and SO validated from my experience with XXXXXXXXXXXXX. I got a head start with the best of the best in our province, Dr. XXXXX! That alone was invaluable. Dr. XXXXX, Dr. XXXXXXX, thank you so much! Both of did so much, in so many ways, I seriously can't thank you enough. Thank you to everyone who contributed to my care from the nurses to the PSW's and porters Huge shoutout and thank you to the amazing nutritionist and truly phenomenal pharmacist who stopped by to talk with me. I have never spoken with a pharmacist or even medical professional who is so non judgmental, open, forward thinking and respectful to others experiences. The level of accommodation offered, had I taken it (I didn't for logistical reasons), was incredibly supportive and validating. Thank you

input: Overall great experience. However the bathroom in my recovery room had a leak that made the floor quite wet and therefore a bit hard to navigate and potentially unsafe. Additionally, I don't think it's necessary for the floor coordinator to be present during delivery or to speak down to the nurses and rushing us out of the delivery room (especially in front of the patient). Lastly, I note that I was asked for consent to participate in a study only a few minutes before being asked to push. I initially consented but then withdrew my consent due to the delay to my delivery that participation in the study was causing. While I felt comfortable withdrawing consent, I don't think it's good practice to ask for consent to participate in a study at that point in the labor and delivery process. Other patients may not fully understand what is involved in participating (as it wasn't fully explained) and may feel that they really don't have a choice. I note that I was told that they would give me a copy of the signed consent after my delivery so that I could read it though fully (ie, was not informed consent). Perhaps consent should be sight through the patient's OB when the patient is in a calm and clear state of mind and when the study can be fully explained.

- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.

- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

input: I am adding this comment for my mother who has dementia. My mother was in the ER for two nights. At the end of that period, she had delirium. The staff seemed overworked. It was very difficult to find a nurse to explain what was going with my mother's care. The doctors never phoned me or contacted me about my mother's health. The staff did a good job restoring my mother's health. But the care wasn't the best. She had only one shower, given by her own PSW during the two week stay. The food was awful. Because of her diagnosis, she was given a minced diet. This was never reviewed until I asked. Then she was given a regular diet. The minced diet was terrible. She was given the same meal every day. I thought I would vomit when I smelt it. She never ate it. Good nutrition would help with a patient's recovery. The staff at the nursing desk weren't helpful. The room seemed clean and new.

input: I have had 7 surgeries in the past 18 months. Some stays were better  than others, communication could have been improved at times. (I was diagnosed as being a diabetic during one of my stays, I was informed of this finding from the kitchen staff) Sometimes the nurses were helpful, other times, not at all. By my 4th visit the nursing staff realized I was a frequent visitor and became friendlier and more helpful. The cleaning staff and the staff that took me down for tests etc. Always treated me with kindness and respect.
