input: Having arrived by myself and being there for 8 hours on a stretcher, it would have been nice if someone had offered me a glass of water a couple of times. After 4 hours I asked for one and for another, later on. also, after 4 hours someone finally noticed that I did not have a pillow and brought me one, I was offered warmed blankets when I arrived, but these were useless after 7 hours. I was freezing. No one came to check and see if I needed anything except when they brought me the pillow. When I was discharged, the nurse did not offer to remove the 'stickers' for the heart monitor, nor remove the electrodes. I did this myself. offered me a pillow.

input: During the pandemic I was not allowed to have someone in with me.  My siblings had to stay outside in the hot sun and fell ill.  Why was I charged fees?  I am a foreigner and was stuck here due to the pandemic.  I had no travel insurance and my sibling had to pay for me. If a Canadian had gone to a hospital in Trinidad (my home), they would not have been charged and likely given free meds because of the pandemic.

input: I found it very upsetting to see and hear the suicide-attempt teenager in the curtained area beside the sitting area (for several hours). Also to see the man in obvious pain who had been told (we could all hear it) by the surgeon that he had acute appendicitis, having to lie on a few chairs to wait for his surgery. Also to see a morbidly obese veteran in his motorized scooter snoring loudly with his mask on his chin - observed by several staff but never told to put the mask on and never seen by any healthcare professionals in the 3 hours that I sat waiting. The results after 8 hours of waiting, having had 2 tests, were given to me by a nurse and not a doctor. I was told approx 1 hr for bloodwork results @ 11 p.m. and got results around 3 a.m. It was exhausting and frustrating.

input: I felt as if Covid wasn't taken seriously considering I had several people sharing my room with me less than 6 feet. Bathrooms were shared and never cleaned during my entire stay. I had to clean other women's blood from the toilet seat and on other surfaces which was difficult to do since I had just given birth hours prior. When I ran my bell, no one came for roughly an hour, at one point I had just gone to the desk on my own to find my nurse on Facebook ... At another point, I had asked for help and my nurse told me I had to figure it out on my own with no one from my family there to help me and it being my first child. Had I of known of another hospital that delivered babies, I would of gone there instead.

Easy fixes  1.  Simple bedside respect (I have never had a surgical procedure where the doctor has not taken a moment to introduced themselves).  2.  Showing some empathy - often the biggest part of healing is acknowledging of a concern.  It is not always about providing any treatment. Nursing communication - I have always (as a XXXXX for 45 year) been taught that never minimize the patients concern over pain.  4.  Timing of the radiologist reporting on the x-rays performed in emergency. I returned by ambulance to XXXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX where I was told by the nurse practitioner, after she consulted with Dr XXXXXXXXXX that my ICD leads had moved and they needed to open me and replace it.  I informed the anesthetist that I was very uncomfortable during the initial surgery and asked if he could insure that I had adequate pain management.  Dr XXXXX did not see me or introduce himself at anytime during or after the surgery.  I was in pain and made it know that I was in pain and I heard someone say they were going to give me more medication which did not improve my comfort.  I could feel the suturing at the end of the removal and insertion of the leads in the RA and coronary sinus.  I was discharged at 8 pm (excellent supportive care by nurses in recovery). input: This hospital experience was the worst of my life (and I have had many). Appalling, in fact. We literally spent 24 STRAIGHT hours in paeds emerg as 'no beds were available' on the floor. Yet went up to the floor eventually to an empty double room ... I gave a FULL history to 9, NINE, people. Not one single person seemed to take the time to look in my son's chart and review anything that was written before proceeding to ask me 10 million questions. 2 people, a senior resident and med student, came to the room at different times with the wrong idea as to why my son was there. 2 people, another resident and med student, came in at one point and because they saw a pink blanket assumed my son was a girl and kept saying 'she'. They later admitted they hadn't even checked the chart yet. It disgusts me how little communication between staff there is, how many inefficiencies there are. WHY people still write paper notes baffles my mind. Stop being so cheap and invest the dollars and time NOW to make one central electronic charting system that EACH AND EVERY care provider takes 3 minutes to look at before coming into my room. And honestly, the nurses were the best of the staff. My complaints lie largely with the physicians, residents, and med students. I get that this is a teaching hospital and I've been there myself being a XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX but this was absolutely ridiculous and I know this is the norm (sadly). Not only is it physically challenging to keep an admitted XX month old baby in a tiny ass emerg room cubical for 24 hours but it's ethically and treatment wise downright unsafe and inappropriate. I also had to go out of my way at least 6 hours into our visit to ask for a crib. No one cared that 2 adults and one baby where trying to contain themselves to a hospital stretcher. No one knew what the plan was for my son nor did they communicate this to us. I had to also go out of my way to track this information down so that I could figure out childcare arrangements for my other child. What a disorganized mess.

The, shared with screamed all the time and when he wasn't screaming he had a bbaatttteery operated car that.was very loud and disruptive. Is there a way to express my gratitude to all involved even if my photo is taken and passed around with note of thanks would be OK? XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX

input: Yes. I have 2 bulging discs in my spine and possibly more damage done since my MRI. I went in for being in pain. Sitting for 30 minutes or more increases that pain tremendously. I waited over 5 hours in the waiting room. I had to eventually stand and wait because the pain was becoming to unbearable. I then waited nearly 30 minutes to see the doctor who did not treat me pain at all but made it worse by having me lay down on the bed and preform leg exercises. I had to leave and go to shoppers drug mart to get treated for my pain. If I choose to come back and have that same doctor see me I will definitely request a different doctor. My previous doctor before this visit was excellent. Not only did he treat my pain with the help of a nurse which I did not even see this visit, but understood my pain and offered to help with my disability claim in which I was waiting for an appointment before filing. I left this visit 10 times worse than I walked in. I am not at all pleased with the help that I got. I brought a script from my doctor dated XXXXXXXXXXXXX for t3s. 60 pills reduce a day. Should have lasted a month but I take them as needed and lasted me until this visit in XXXX. This doctor who knows nothing about me disagreed because he is uncomfortable prescribing it and in stead gave me a prescription for 3 different meds. Tylenol which was 10 t3s with out the codeine, naproxen which I explained to my doctor does not help with the pain and morphine which I have never done before. With these three prescriptions i was still in tremendous pain. If I have a script which I have been on for over a year know why can't I get that refilled. I ended up taking these 3 different medicines only for my stomach to hurt and the pain of my back remain. This doctor I saw was an amateur I'm sure. I will definitely not want to see him ever again!

input: The only comments that I would like to share are those: Second visit in emerg: all good; but was left in new wing corridor for lack of space; bright lights that the nurses couldn't control; stretcher right under speakers; these are unavoidable; the nurse even gave me earplugs. I felt like a useless lump of meat. And there was no passing by in that hallway other than staff unrelated to me as a patient; no nurses coming to check on me. I even stopped one person at some point who turned out to be a cleaning supervisor to ask her to wave for a nurse (they were scare to pass by). She was not pleasant, uncaring and asked coldly (and obviously annoyed by the intrusion - or that's not my job) what that was all about; i just asked her to get a nurse. No acknowledgement or courtesy but she walked back to the nursing station.

input: There were two main issues with my hospital stay. The first was that the pediatrician did not come to see my newborn baby the day after delivery, this required that we stay in hospital for another day. The frustrating thing with this was that the nurses did not believe me and told me that I was mistaken and that the pediatrician did see me. The charge nurse even came to tell me I was mistaken, which I was not. After this was finally looked into, the pediatrician called me and confirmed that she missed seeing my baby and apologized. The nursing staff should do a better job of listening to their patients when they identify a concern rather than brushing them off. The second issue was with a lactation consultant. The first one who came to see me was rushed and did not listen to my concerns and did not do a proper assessment. She failed to identify that I was engorged and my child had lost nearly 10% of their birth weight which is concerning.  I requested another assessment and the second lactation consultant was amazing and provided very helpful guidance. The hospital should review their staff to ensure that they are performing a good quality job and ensure that there is adequate staffing so they do not cut assessments short.

input: phone call from the Cardiologist (who never called their numbers because the contact information was not typed into the computer or listed on the chart). My son said their phones were on all night.   My stay in CICU was good. The nurses were very attentive, and the Cardiologists were very good at explaining things to me and my family. While in CICU, the Palliative Care doctor (Dr. XXXXXXXXXXX) visited me. She was consulted by Dr. XXXXXXXX to be part of my care team to help with pain management. Dr. XXXXX was very nice and took time to have a private chat with me and my family. Her resident was also very good. Dr. XXXXX listened to everyone's concerns, and capably helped family members who were struggling with decisions related to my care. Dr. XXXXX also listened to me and I felt like she really cared.   After I left CICU, I was moved to a ward room on Cardiology Unit. My care there was pretty good. The nurses that I had were very busy, but my needs were met quite well. It was a bit noisy in that room, but I was able to sleep OK.   Then I was moved to C2 Medical Oncology. By this time, my care was being coordinated by Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, who was very kind and caring. My family never got to meet her, but she called them regularly with updates, and like Dr. XXXXX, would return their phone calls and answer any questions related to my care. I felt that overall the doctors at XXXXXXXXXX were very good and they all seemed to work well together, communicating well between them to coordinate my care efficiently.   XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX has been my health care home for at least 15 years. Most of my Specialists are at XXXXXXXXXX, including my Oncologists, Dr. XXXXXXXXXXX and Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. I always felt listened to by Dr. XXX, who was very attentive and good at explaining things to me and my son-in-law (who sometimes accompanied me to my outpatient clinic appointments). Dr. XXXXXXXXXX was very knowledgeable and good at explaining things, too.   However, when I asked about being referred to the Palliative Care Team last year, after I was diagnosed with bone cancer, they both told me that I was not ready for that yet. At that time, they had given me a longer prognosis. However, it turns out that I could have been plugged into the outpatient Palliative Care Team at any point after being diagnosed with advanced cancer, but because I had agreed to be part of their research trial, I was not able to access symptom and pain management care provided by the outpatient Palliative Care Team. My family disagrees with this, and were told by the Palliative Care Team at XXXXXXXXXX that anyone can access their services anytime during their cancer journey, as they do not just deal with imminent dying, but also pain and symptom management during the illness. It may help other patients if the XXXXXXXXXXXXX knows this and can refer patients who request palliative care management as outpatients. It seems that the research doctors only focus on the treatment of the cancer, but my family suggests that perhaps they could take a more holistic approach and include the family earlier in the treatment process, and plug their patients into the palliative care outpatient services earlier, in order to help the patient cope with the other aspects of cancer, not just the drug trial.   Despite the size of the hospital, the communication seems to be pretty efficient, particularly between physicians. One suggestion that my family has, though, is to ensure that each department updates their family contact information as part of their overall assessment, and include the names and contact information for family members, particularly the POAs, as part of their routine admission procedures. My family had to initiate providing updated information in each department including Admitting and Patient Accounts, and they did find that each department seems to do things differently, but perhaps a streamlined computer process from Admitting to each unit would improve communtion with family members (i.e. POAs).   Also, my family suggests that staff should always include the POAs in important discussions about Advanced Directives and other decisions (such as emergency procedures), as well as with the patient.   Another suggestion is to improve your patient Porter services. There seems to be a shortage of porters in the hospital; I was late for some appointments in various departments during my stay because the porter was either called too late or came late. Some of this was because the Ward Clerks told my family that the outpatient clinic appointments (i.e. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) are not connected to the inpatient computer system, hence they rely on family members to contact the inpatient unit themselves to inform the Ward Clerk/nurses of clinic appointments for regular clinic outpatients who are now hospitalized. Also, my family discovered that sometimes the outpatient clinic appointments are not accurately displayed in the XXXXXXXXXX online appointment calendar, which seems to only be accessible by patients like myself. They had to scramble one day to get me to a pre-booked outpatient appointment at the Radiation Clinic at XXXXXX because one family member happened to call the office and were informed of this important appointment.   As a result, my family discovered that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX has no way of knowing if their outpatients are hospitalized at XXXXXXXXXX, so they  rely on patients or family members to inform them so that the patient does not miss appointments, or changes need to be made to pre-booked outpatient clinic appointments. Could your IT departments at XXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX work together to streamline computer communication between the Admitting department and the Outpatient Clinics, so when an XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX outpatient is hospitalized, the clinic would receive an electronic flag in their system? Also, can your IT hospital department fix the apparent disconnect between unit computers, as each time I moved my family had to update their contact information with each Ward clerk.   The place is very clean and well-organized, with good signage directing patrons to the various departments throughout the massive building. However, my family asked if you could please add a sign to the exit door on H Wing that leads outside towards K Wing? The signs directing visitors that direction seem to end part way up that hall, and then my family did not know where to go. Also, it is almost impossible to find the Admitting and Patient Accounts offices.   Overall, my family and I believe that XXXXXXXXXX is an amazing health care facility. The doctors are top-notch and most of the nurses are very caring and kind and professional. I felt like I was treated with respect and dignity, and included in my care planning the entire time I was in the hospital. The Social Workers on each of the units were very nice, too, as were the other health care professionals.  My family and I would rate XXXXXXXXXX with a 9 out of 10, and we would highly recommend your hospital to anyone.   Thank you.I was originally admitted to ER on XXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXX at around supper time, when my son-in-law drove me to XXXXXXXXXX ER at my request. Unfortunately, despite my family's verbal objections clearly stating that I was unsafe to return home and needed to be properly assessed, the Geri RN/DIscharge Nurse in ER that evening insisted that I could return home even though the doctor had not yet seen me. That RN argued with my family on the phone (my son is POA) and she said 'since I was having surgery the next morning and would be admitted overnight afterwards, that I could just go home and they would deal with this when you are admitted.' She also said that 'there was no point in me staying in ER overnight, as I would not get a good sleep before my surgery.'  The ER doctor on XXXXXXXX spent 10 minutes asking some questions of me and my son-in-law. I was sent home (I live alone) after a short ER visit (i.e. a couple of hours), even though I came to hospital because I could barely walk and was in severe pain from my condition, with weakness and not feeling well (I have cancer in my spine). The ER doctor on XXXXXXXX evening barely examined me, and gave me a dose of stronger pain medication (narcotic), which I have never taken before, right before I was sent home. The RN did give me a walker and had me walk around the room, but they never did any tests. I returned to XXXXXXXXXX ER the next morning at 6:30 a.m. via ambulance from home, because I fell in the night and my family found me on the floor.   While I was in ER on XXXXXXXX, I waited 4 hours to be seen by a doctor, and was only seen initially by a Physician Assistant (who was very nice) after my family came at 11 a.m. and asked for me to be seen by a doctor. The ER nurses were very nice on XXXXXXXX, and once I was assessed, Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (Medical Oncology Internal Medicine) and his wonderful Resident took over my care. They were amazing, very thorough, were very caring and concerned, listened attentively to my concerns and my family's concerns, and did numerous tests to  find out why I was in so much pain and could not walk/was very weak (which is why I came to hospital on XXXXXXXX and returned on XXXXXXXX, just 12 hours later). My family were very impressed with Dr. XXXXXXXX.   Dr. XXXXXXXX ordered a heart monitor (I have a heart history, including heart bypass 15 years ago at XXXXXXXXXX), and he agreed with my family that I was unsafe to return home and he admitted me to hospital. I had to stay in ER on a stretcher overnight in the hall next to the nurse's station, but I was comfortable and felt well cared for. To everyone's surprise (including me), my heart rate dropped during the wee hours on XXXXXX XXXXXXXX, and I was rushed to Cardiac Catheter Lab for an emergency temporary pacemaker insertion. I remember being woken up during a good sleep to be told my heart was not working properly and I needed a pacemaker. My family discovered two days later that they were never consulted by ER staff, after my family left at 3:30 p.m. on XXXXXXXX (having been there all day with me), to discuss the Advanced Directives form that I was asked about by myself at 4:30 p.m. on XXXXXXXX. That form was later shown to my family in CICU and it indicated that I had agreed to electrical implant if needed, and I chose DNR, DNI because I have terminal cancer.   Even though the Cardiologist who assessed me in ER that night (XXXXXXXX at 2:30 a.m.) claimed that she called various family members, only my son-in-law's phone number was called during the night (his cell phone is turned off at night) because it was discovered that his contact information was the only information in the computer from my first ER visit on XXXXXXXX. My son and his wife had given the ER staff a typed list of up-to-date contact information on XXXXXXXX at 11 a.m. when they arrived in ER, which included my son and daughter-in-law's cell numbers (they had come into the city overnight), but neither of them ever got the emerge

Some physio???s are great, but some physio assistants give a patient an exercise to do in the gym then sit down & play with their smart phones ??? why is there not proper supervision of lower level staff? Even small details (eg a paper towel dispenser in the washrooms) are neglected ??? the dispenser cannot be readied easily from a wheelchair, & the towels take a huge effort to remove thus again, XXXXXXXXXXX goes to great lengths to pat itself on the back, without actually checking that services are properly delivered or maintained. More of the budget could be directed to maintenance & supervision and less toward self congratulating promotion branding.

input: I brought my X month old daughter to the emergency room on the recommendation of XXXXXXXXXX. She had a high fever, refused to eat, was vomiting and diarrhea. The emergency doctor completely dismissed my concerns and made me feel like an idiot for being worried. I was never asked about her eating/drinking, how many wet diapers she had etc. With a sick infant, dehydration should be important. The doctor spent MAYBE 5 mins with us. Checked her eyes, listened to her chest for a second and told me it was just viral and to go home to wait it out. He didn't ask me any questions. Never checked her soft spot. Never checked her ears. Never did an xray. The following morning I had an appointment with her pediatrician. From the doctors office she sent us immediately to the 4th floor where the nurses were waiting for IV hydration at the hospital because she could tell my daughter was very dehydrated. She ended up testing positive for Influenza A and an xray showed chest infection/pneumonia. Thank god I went to see her doctor because if not, who knows what could have happened. The care I received in the ER was DESPICABLE! I have had countless horrible experiences at the XXXXXXXXXXXXX hospital with my children (my XX month old son waited 6 hours in the waiting room with a dislocated arm and the nurses wouldn't even give him tylenol for the pain... try explaining to a XX month old why he cant move his arm or it will hurt...) and the only reason I brought my daughter there was because I could not make the drive to XXXXXXXXX orXXXXXXXXX with her in the back alone because she was vomiting.

input: The nurses and doctors were terrific and did the best they could. Unfortunately the nurses are run off their feet and you need to hire more nurses. They had to deal with unruly patients as well as take care of those in their charge. My room was just outside of the nurses station and those bells went off all day and all night - that would drive me crazy but they managed to handle it very well. Unfortunately I didn't get much sleep but that was not their fault. When I went into the hospital I was totally helpless and they made me feel as secure as they could and explained everything that they were going to be doing before they did it and, I appreciated that very much. I have never been so helpless in my entire life and they took very good care of me up until I could go home and take care of myself again!

input: My emergency room visits were somewhat unusual. I had a surgical wound that had become infected and the surgeon who was treating me had me admitted through emergency so that I would have surgery (debridement) later in the day. This happened three times. The waits were very long, the longest being something like 15 hours. This was not due to the emergency room but rather because it took that long to schedule the surgery. The medical team in the emergency room did what they could to make me comfortable and treat the infected area while I was waiting. I brought my Kindle so I could minimize the frustration. The waiting was a difficult experience but the team in the emergency room were not at fault.

input: First of all, the waiting times were astronomically long. The nursing staff definitely seemed to be caring for the patients as best they could, though I did not see nurses very often either, not sure if they were short staffed or if this was the norm. The doctor himself was never around, I waited well over 2 hours for results from a scan, only to finally track down a nurse who said that the results were ready half an hour after the test was completed. The follow-up from the doctor was that I needed to see a specialist. After spending all night in the hospital, and being under the impression that the specialist would be arriving in the morning, I was then told that I would need to drive to the North end of XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, despite not being able to drive myself. I was put in a bed in the corner of the ER at about 6am, which appeared to be a storage area. I felt very much like an inconvenience for the staff. Even asking one of the nurses in the morning for a Kleenex box seemed to be too much to ask for. I was not given any prescriptions for pain medication, despite being in agonizing pain.

input: I was taken by ambulance to emergency high ever, vomiting, blood sugars increase 24. Emerg was very busy at night & TV & drinking fluids. I had to go to the B room frequently. I was told to unplug pump, 02 stayed & one other instruction (can't remember) with high fever etc I couldn't get the instructions correct & had to ask the nurse repeatedly for help I explained how I felt, & was told how restless I was (I knew this) This increased anxiety I have never been incontinent, but was trying to figure out instructions, & yes had an accident - It was not a good night! My perineum became raw! The skin came off & yes it was painful! I was treated with cream, IV, meds etc but on discharge I ended up on the IV at home & celluctis It is XXXXX, & I'm finally draining My doctor & other staff - fantastic I only wish the nurse had not assumed I could to the IVe pump etc. especially when I explained I couldn't take it all in. I had never felt this helpless before & yes it bothered me very much This abrasion to the perineum was a side effect I didn't go in with It has also prolonged my recovery Yes, it was only 1 person, but I will never forget this I felt so sick, I felt so much anxiety, I felt helpless, I felt discouraged, I was angry But, I didn't complain I didn't want to be a problem patient on a night shift When I went to the floor it was better & I'm thankful to the doctor & staff I believe you can't teach empathy but as a professional you are taught to try & meet the needs Thank you for reading this & listening I am a retired RN. PS With high BIS, fever, sweating & "accident" I feel this could have been prevented I did return to emerg & there was a question of a perineum abscess & I was stared on antibiotic drip -> continued @ home VON - fantastic support!

input: When we arrived at the ER, I was initially impressed because the registration process was quick and we were led to the patient room right away. We also appreciated that each patient has his/her own little room.  The nurses and doctors were courteous. My son and I also appreciated that they looked at my son directly in the eyes and were very patient in answering my son's questions and in explaining to him what was happening.  Everyone was polite and understanding once we got to speak to them. The problem was it took too long to get tests done and it just took way too long to get any care at all. We had to wait for hours to get wheeled to the ultrasound area, and a few more hours to get wheeled back to the emergency room. Moreover, several hours went by without anyone coming to explain to us what was happening or what we should be expecting next.  The whole night, we were waiting, but no one came to explain. I had to go out of my way and ask the nurse for updates before I was able to obtain some form of information. And the following day, I had to follow up again and wait a few more hours before the doctor came and provided the diagnosis. And once we were informed that we can go home, we had to wait another 2 hours and it took another follow up before a doctor came and cleared us to leave.  Also, in the beginning, when we arrived, I had to answer the same questions multiple times because the nurses or other staff who came to the room asked exactly the same questions.  It just seemed like they were not recording the answers or the medical team did not review the patient profile before coming into the room. Our family appreciates all the effort and care that the doctors, nurses, staff and the whole XXXXXXXX team provide patients daily.  However, overall patient care time needs to be improved. Our hospital visit should not have taken us more than 16 hours. Thank you for allowing us to provide our feedback.

input: I was in the Neurosurgery Inpatient Ward. The nurse named XXXXXXXX was an exceptional individual. She made all patients feel like they weren't even admitted to the hospital. She was willing to assist in any means and was always uplifting the mood. I have never met such a lovely medical staff like her in my life. Likewise the physiotherapist, surgeon, and anesthesiologist were also fantastic individuals. Everyone was willing to answer any questions and make this experience very comfortable. The only complaint were the two other patients that I shared the room with during my stay. The first individual continuously spoke on the phone loudly, while the second individual watched TV at a high volume. This greatly affected my ability to sleep. But I understand this has nothing to do with XXXXXXXXXXX's hospital and it's process. Overall, I am extremely happy with my stay. Hats off to the medical staff at this hospital.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I am not from XXXXXXX. I was flown to XXXXXXXXXXX as an emergency. Therefore, my admission and stay could not have been planned. My baby was immediately sent to XXXXXXXXX after a very short labor and delivery (30 minutes). There was not much 'post-natal' care given (i.e. breastfeeding, bathing baby, etc.) because I was very ill and the focus was on figuring out what was going on with me and how to treat it. I very much appreciated all the work and concern from all teams (i.e. obs, hematology, nephrology, ICU, etc.). My only recommendations would be to have had a social worker check in on me and my family and a reminder that there was a 'alternate' menu to order from. Bland 'chicken' , rice and fruit cups got boring. My stay was a total of 17 days. A more 'ecological' point: I don't believe all the plastic trays and Styrofoam bowls were necessary (ex: I got an apple every day in a foam bowl, my condiments were in plastic trays...). Very damaging for the environment.

input: I was very disappointed with the care I received at XXXXXXXXXXXX. Although I have nothing but great things to say about XXXXXXXXXX and his surgical team, the care I received as an in patient was unacceptable. My biggest complaint (I have a few) was the pain management protocol. I was taken off the pump the morning of my discharge, and left the hospital with my pain level at an 8. I was unable to bend my knee to sit in the wheelchair (I had a total knee replacement two days earlier). I was obviously in distress as it took three nurses to try to get I the chair. I had an hour drive home and the nurse told my husband to lay in the back seat. The pain I felt on that drive home was unbearable as was my pain level for the next week or so. I feel that this has slowed down my healing process. Is there not a pain management protocol wherein patients have to have their pain controlled before discharge? This is especially important with a knee replacement as you have to push through pain during Physio. End of my rant....

input: I had surgery and was roomed with a mental health patient with a steady stream of visitors.  Nursing staff were "OK."  One was awesome - XXXXX or XXXX I believe  Meal choices post surgery were heavy - battered soggy fish and fries  Overcooked eggs  Dr didn't visit post op until I asked and wanted to go home to rest in quiet. As a single mom I have faced some adversity as a result of things that happened to us.  It being a small town, I realize that narrow minded ignorance is still alive and well in XX and XXXXXXX.  Staff would do well to take some cultural difference and acceptance training & learn decorum  * Respect, basic human rights

input: Everything was perfect except for the constipation associated with the meds and the anesthetic. There needs to be more focus on fiber. Prune juice instead of apple. Some laxative with each pain med. After leaving the hospital I was in agony and humiliation for two days trying to get my system back into gear. When I left the hospital I had no information about post surgery services available to me in the community. I had no information about what was available. I made my own (bad) arrangements at a senior residence thinking that was what I needed - alone, single, no kids. That was horrible because they were not geared to help me - no physio, only responding to my inquiries, not offering any support or help. I felt I did not have the right help or information for after the hospital. Truly, I felt neglected, nervous and depressed when I left. Much better now.

input: It was challenging to have so many healthcare workers come to the room unannounced or unplanned throughout the day . Meal services were sometimes delivered much later than expected with little time to finish the meal before the tray was collected again.  We had issues with our water in the room sink and bathroom turning brown several times during our stay. We understand there was work being done on the roof, however it made washing, bathing and feeding our newborn difficult. The water pressure in the shower was so low that it was almost unusable.

instruction:
You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I went to XXXXXXX's in XXXXXXXXXXXX within 30 minutes of the fall. I was crying from pain & out of breath and I did not have the strength to stand, so I was given a chair by another patient. I asked if I could please be seen right away in fear that I may have ruptured something. The triage nurse said, 'what about all these people before you.' I was made to wait an hour. When I did get in the nurse told me to put on a gown and left. I tried to called after her, but she did not return. The nurse was there shortly to take me for xrays, and she helped me take off my top and bra so I could put on the gown. The doctor was good and I was treated right away once I was in emergency, but because of the triage nurse I will it go back there if I can help it.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh
input: I feel like the nursing care was lacking, I understand the need for no visitors during the pandemic but my husband received no updates even after he called. The only message I got, was a clerk that walked by me and said your husband called. The clerk apparently told my husband I would call him and I was unaware of this. He was home with my children worried with no idea of what was happening to me. All the x-ray and CT technicians were very pleasant and I was very happy with my doctors care. When it came time to go home I felt like I was rushed out, I was to wait for surgery for a few days, was told that I could change into a gown and they would help me put my arm in a sling. After the nurse helped me change and put the sling on he exited my room, when I sat up I was shaking, sweating and began to vomit. He came back a few minutes later and asked why I was still here I explained how I was feeling and he said OK I'm going to get you a wheelchair. I was put in the chair still feeling unwell and wheeled out the door to my waiting husband. I realize rooms are needed for other people but I felt like it didn't matter how I was feeling, it was time to go. I returned to the ER a few days later, the day of my surgery. My nerve block had worn off 12 hours early and I've never been in so much pain in my life. I explained to the triage nurse that I had medication but I was following the doctors orders and was taking it as prescribed. This medication was not even touching the pain, I was sat in the waiting room for 4 1/2 hours crying and writhing the entire time, I felt like I wasn't listened to and that my pain didn't matter. The first time in my life I understood why people could get addicted to narcotics, I remained vigilant through the pain and didn't take any extra. It was inhumane!! As an employee of the hospital I was very saddened to see how I was treated in the ER and I didn't make me proud at all!!

input: Every time I went it was always a different experience. I was in a tremendous amount of pain so much so that I was almost crawling. I seen many different doctors and to this day have no clue what's wrong. First it was my appendix, then kidney stones. Every doc was different. However I was given anything for my pain and discomfort when I left each time I am well aware of the drug "crisis" that is occurring from town to town city to city. However I clearly needed something and each time I was given nothing to go home with. So I sat hours on hours, time off work, stated my pain each time I went and asked each time please please may I have something. Each time was "no." So back to emerge I went the next day in hopes of an answer or something. As a patient I was neglected in that sense. I don't usually take anything for pain but this time was clearly a time I needed it. The nurses I had were wonderful. The doctors seemed to be rushed. If I was there more than one time then clearly something was wrong. The nurses knew me by name. I wish they would of listened to me when I said I was in pain and needed something for my pain I didn't need a lesson on the "drug epidemic" that is happening. Your the doctor listen to your patient. I don't do drugs not a druggie so your opinion on it meant nothing to me I was there for medical attention and felt I didn't receive it.

So we paid for 3 hours of parking and wasted my and my wife's time.  NOT IMPRESSED

When I was sent home from ER to wait for a call back, I was told to stay NPO and taht someone will call me at 8am in the morning and tell me if I will have an operation that day I was suppose to stay NPO until I received the call No one called me Finally at noon, was I was starving, I managed to get a hold of the resident who had seen me the night before and he told me to eat since I will not be operated on I was told to stay NPO after midnight and that someone will call me the next day at 8am Again no one called me! I had to make a lot of calls to hospital until I figured out that I can eat breakfast then stay NPO Again no one called me I finally got a hold of OR booking and was told that it was my turn and the charge nurse didn't know that I was home!!! I had to rush to hospital at 8pm!! Again from the moment I entered OR until my discharge the care was amazing

input: Both parents stayed with our daughter overnight following surgery. My daughter was the only patient in the room. There was one small bed for a parent. We asked for another bed for the additional parent, as there were multiple beds in the hallway. We were told that was not possible. One parent had to sleep sitting up in the chair. In the morning another bed was brought in. It was frustrating that we could not have an extra parent bed (there were 8 in the hallway lined up not being used). Our assigned nurse indicated she would bring one in for the other parent. The charge nurse was overheard declining this request and suggested a parent sleep in the playroom. This was not patient or family centered care.

input: I was there with my husband the day after XXXXXXXXXXXX. I had severe back pain and I found it difficult to walk. I called for ambulance service as I was afraid I would fall and I had already broken a hip two years earlier. The ambulance attendants were wonderful and made me feel that they would make sure that I wouldn't fall. I was checked in at the hospital and put in a line up for the Triage nurse .I was seen by the Triage nurse and then was left in the same line for several hours. Eventually I was taken to an area to see a Doctor. Seemingly the triage nurse had left instructions as to my care. The instructions got misplaced and didn't become available until the evening and I was told my x-rays and blood work should have been looked after around two o'clock in the p.m. It was now around 6:30 p.m. The Doctor apologized for the long wait time and then things started to get done. He had just come on duty and we were able to leave the hospital around 8:30 approx. The nurses that did the blood work and x-rays were very caring but during my whole stay I didn't seem to have anybody checking on me routinely. No one identified themselves as being in charge of my care. I did ask a nurse to help me with obtaining a pillow in the Triage line and I was told she was not my nurse and she pointed way down the hall to a cluster of beings as if that would be where I would get help. I ended up putting my purse under my head until a kind ambulance attendant found me a pillow. The only people making you feel that you were in a friendly place were the cleaning staff who sometimes would smile at you as they did their important chores. I would recommend that more smiles be passed around even if they have to be faked. Smiles relieve stress and benefit all including patients and staff.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: 1. During my transfer from emergency to my hospital room, my shoes were lost. They had been placed on the rack below the gurney used to transport me by the attendant moving me and they were not removed when I arrived at the room. I, and also my wife, made inquiries over the next 2 days to try to find them but to no avail.  My wife had to bring me another pair when I was discharged.  2.  I was in the newest part of the hospital and the room and facilities were very good.  However the bathroom was allowed to become quite dirty (not from me or the other patient in the room).  I can't say it affected my stay negatively, but it was disappointing when everything else was quite good. (I do realize during this pandemic it is difficult for everyone, even the cleaning staff, who are occupied doing a lot more disinfecting than in normal times)

input: The admitting process was a bit tiring for us - we were in for observation for 8 hours on XXXXX and then sent home with a Foley and asked to come back after a call, which we expected at 8 pm we called at 10:30 and were told to come back in. The following day XXXXXX we were admitted and then our nurse was pulled from our care 2x that day (due to other emergencies as far as I understand). So after waiting almost 8 hours we started the induction process. On XXXXXX we worked though the induction process and everything went as well as possible. On XXXXXX while in labor we had some issues with a nurse on our care team who neglected to refill my epidural drip and I woke up in extreme pain, this was addressed quickly by the other nurses on my team as well as the anesthesiologist. At that same time it was noted that I had an infection due to my water being broken for an extended period of time, I wish that this was monitored more closely as it was terrifying to not understand what was happening so close to giving birth. All in all our doctors and nurses were wonderful in listening to our concerns and working with us to have a vaginal delivery. PS. Our nurse XXXX who we had for two shifts was amazing!

input: The only complaint about stay at XXX was the person I was in the room with. She was a young woman and her boyfriend moved in her for the night. The lights were on the whole night and they were watching movies. And I had to ask the couple to turn lights off. I was up the whole night. I told the nurse about it and she said it was the 24/7 policy. The head nurse who came in the following day was annoyed with the visitor sharing the bed with the patient. That was a very bad experience at XXX. I don't think the 24 7 policy is good for patients getting treatment since there is no control over anybody coming and going.

input: All of the hospitals in Eastern XXXXXXX joining together at a higher level. Went to the hospital and pretty certain having a heart attack. They sent me to the heart institute. They did what they usually do. Upon arrival did the procedure that needed to be done. Next time I woke up I may have been in XXXXXXX something people should know that when in a hospital in Eastern XXXXXXX they keep asking what day is it and where are you. That is a tough question. I woke up in a different place every day until I got to XXXXXXXX and got no sleep. Really unsettling they put you in the ambulance and drop you off someplace. They need to tell what they are doing. I got a letter saying I was confused. Damn right I was confused because of lack of sleep and where the hell I was taken to. This was an ugly experience in my mind. That has a lot to do with the organization the hospitals belong too. The covers you experience in the hospital. When I got home it took awhile to get sleep properly. They send in a prescription with 15 items on it. Take one twice daily. Take a quarter of one twice one 3 or 4 mm wide and 1 or 2 mm long. Hard to cut that. Have a whole bunch of pills not sure when to take them. Turns out 4 of the 15 mess with your sleep. 1. They have to be more specified when they write prescription. Hard time to figure it out. The pills you get possibly for 2 or 3 exceptions do not look the same as you got in the hospital. That is a problem could lead to all kinds of problems. I think it is important that you get a list of your prescriptions and when to take them. Once daily is not answer. Causes a lot of grief. Do not have a definitive answer on when to take them. At the heart institute some guy inform me he was going to put me on a drug that caused me to black out. One of the problems why I could not sleep my roommate would call out in the night and the nurses did not do anything.

input: Overall I am pleased with the treatment and services received here at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. Just want to provide some thoughts while we are admitted to hospital for a few days now. was Patient needs rest and quiet atmosphere most of the time. Example 1: One night, not seeing any emergency issue, my baby (X month old) was disturbed every one hour because of the nurse came in do her check duties and X-ray during midnight and some nurse who is not responsible to her come to randomly check her out without any contribution to her treatment. I think the vital check should be reasonable and coordinate with patient's resting schedule. Some nurses are very professional, careful and organized and able to do the check while making less disturbance. I suggest always communicate with parents about the plan and what they will be expected on the plan.  Example 2: I don't want to feel like I am in a Zoo while a group of people just come in and everyone come and examine my baby while she was already not feeling well. I prefer a group of two to three people and there should be a communication of plan.

input: I did not have a baby during my hospital stay. I tried to ignore this survey initially for that reason but I kept receiving emails, so I only answered the questions that applied to my hospital stay. I had surgery and was placed on that unit. The nurses were pleasantly and helpful.  I was the only patient in the room which was why the room was so quiet and peaceful. The only negative thing was that I was not given enough information or guidance about buying products to combat constipation. My friend who is a XXXXX told me to purchase stool softeners etc and said that is common practice. During my stay at the hospital  I was given laxative drink and stool softener pill but was only prescribed opioids with no information about the consequences of severe constipation which I suffered thereafter. In conclusion, I had an excellent stay primarily because the room was so quiet and I was able to sleep. Also the nurses were professional,attentive and friendly. They genuinely showed their concern and care for my recovery. There were no questions about the food, but the food was good which always helps.

input: There's inexplicably high wait time to see doctors. I go to a hospital not to have a good interaction, but only prompt and comprehensive care. If there's no one waiting, I'm more than happy to talk to everyone. But given the number of people waiting and suffering, I am ok if the doctor rapidly asks me diagnostically relevant questions, makes a decision and moves on to other patients. I guess, this is a systemic problem, perhaps not specific to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. It's painful to know that there're ways to serve a lot more patients in much less time and with a lot less facilities. The doctors and nurses I met were very nice though, so thanks for that! The standard of care is diminished considerably if it's preceded by a 3 hour wait.

input: (1) We have been coming to the hospital for 2 years. Never once have the nurses been able to get in the IV. I always ask for the IV team but I always get push back. The nurses who have been trained on IV are still not proficient in it. They also feel stressed that they have to try & this causes more pain and stress on my child. I propose all young children automatically get the IV team use the resources to create a second IV team instead of training nurses. It's better to have experts that jack of all trades. (2) Children getting needles should automatically receive the numbing spray as protocol to reduce pain. (3) All covid tests should be the cheek and nose or spit test to decrease pain on children. (4) All information about rare side effects when and why to inform the child should be printed out. (5) Brings toys to distract kids. Child life should be introduced immediately to families their first stay they are wonderful! (6) parents should be given suggestions on how to decrease needed anxiety. (7) When prescribing medicine like steroids the amount of liquid should be taken into account the less liquid the easier for the child. (8) My son is X and can swallow a huge pill. This is great info and could be shared at a staff meeting. (9) My son needed N tube our nurse was wise to ask another nurse who was an expert in inserting them to focus on using experts is very important to reduce pain and stress on children. Parents should be told realistic timelines of how long procedures will take as much as possible, it's better to say longer than less. During one of our first stays a wonderful nurse included my son in the vitals process pressing buttons choosing which arm to use for blood pressure, this really helped my son feel positive about experience and she taught me how important it is to include him. Windows should be able to open with covid info and all the other stressors they go through the hospital this is imperative. I would love to see more diverse staff on the nurse roster. It is glaringly obvious the staff is majority white. Nurse should get paid more and get more breaks! They are amazing! The staff at XXXXXXXXX are wonderful. So caring and hard working. Attentive, loving. We are so grateful.

input: I just found an extreme difference between my care and the care of people who were older and may be mentally incapacitated. I had seen a person who had been there a very long time and they had horrible care. I almost felt embarrassed at the care I was receiving as a younger and more mentally sound person. It was very upsetting. There was one nurse in particular that should have been fired. I made a comment to another nurse and she agreed with me. I understand where they were coming from because the frustration was great but that's what they sign up for. It can't all be patients that are easy to get along with. I don't know what the solution is but I found it very upsetting. It's sad that our seniors and people who have mental problems are treated that way. My care was excellent but that is not the care that I saw this other patient get.

input: I would like to say that time and time again, anytime I had to visit XXX (both XXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXX Campuses), I have always had a good experience. They are my home hospitals and I have been there to have 3 children, my family has had to be admitted there, my children has visited the ER, and most recently myself had to be admitted. The staff have always gone above and beyond and if they were not able to, it was for good reason or we were always attended to as soon as they were free. During this admission, the ER staff and the staff on 4D were so great. I still have yet to send them a thank you gift as I'm still recovering, but hopefully I will soon. They always talked to us in a respectful manner and never talked to us as if we didn't know anything. If they were unable to answer, they would contact the physician and relay messages. They would always try their best to accommodate me. This goes to all the staff: nurses, physicians, specialists, porters, ultrasound/MRI/X-ray technicians, phlebotomists, service staff, cleaners...EVERYONE. So thank you for making my most recent admission just as comfortable, since it was a scary time for me. Staff I'd like to name: ER - Dr. XXXXX, Dr. XXXXXX (sp?), XXXXX, XXX, XXXXX; 4D staff - XXXXX, DR. XXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXX, Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXX, XXXXXXXX, XXXXXXX, XXXXXX, XXXXXXXXX, XXXXX. That's not even the full list, but I wanted to at least provide those I did remember. Thank you for your time!

input: The doctor told me to suck up my pain (Dr. XXXXX) and when he looked at my MRI, he just said there is nothing wrong with it, prescribed me Percocet and told me to move on with my life.  All the doctor did was perform a rectal exam and bladder ultrasound and dismissed me. The doctor was also extremely unprofessional and rude and really made my first emergency visit feel like the worst experience and I never wanted to return to another hospital in my life. I was not sure what I had done wrong for the doctor to treat me like this and figured that the doctor just did not like me when I saw him talking to his other patients with care and respect while treating me like garbage. It was also very entertaining to see that he spent half his time flirting with the nurses and other nurses. To be honest, I never feel like this but I felt like I was racially profiled by the doctor, but I do not want to jump to conclusions. When my family doctor originally called me, he was extremely worried as he looked at my MRI and required me to go to the emergency at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX due to my urinary incontinence (at XX years old). The next day after my visit, my pain was getting worse to the point where I couldn't walk at all and my XXXX was urging me to go to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX for emergency again - I did not want to leave my room after my experience with the doctor at XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. When I went to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, they looked at my MRI (after my XXXX came to get my CD from XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) and they took very good care of me, listened and worked with me to get the treatment I needed. I was booked with a Neurosurgeon and Orthopaedic Surgeon to get appropriate advice on my severely bulging herniated disc. Both surgeons told me that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX should not have dismissed me and that the doctor that dismissed me should not have been so ignorant of my condition (especially because I was experiencing urinary incontinence) and told me that I urgently needed surgery. My surgery is now booked for XXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXX (2 days from today) and I will never be returning to XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.  I have already told all of my friends and family - they all agreed that based on their previous experiences, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is one of the worst, if not, the worst hospital in the entire XXX. Next time I require an emergency, I'm going to XXXXXXXXX or XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX - forget XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. If you would like to contact me to further discuss my visit, please feel free to do so through my email or call me on my cell phone (preferably email). Thank you for your time.

input: I know that the staff are all busy, but sometimes it can be VERY reassuring to a patient of the status of things. Even to have a nurse put their heads in the door and just simply say, 'we're just waiting for your labs still to come back' or any sort of update while waiting would be SO GREATLY appreciated. When a patient has to sit there for hours on end and in pain, we're usually tense or scared of what's going on and that simple update or touching base with the patient would really be calming and helpful. Or to even say, 'Are you ok? Do you want a warm blanket?' as it's ALWAYS freezing in the ER dept. I'm thankful that I have an ER that I can go to that's nearby, especially when it's so hard to get in with doctors these days. Thanks.

One nurse kept me company (which I really appreciated) and tried to get somebody in to help with the pain, but it took too long. The first time I had a XXXXXXXX in XXXX it was handled much better.

input: Visited hospital since exhibiting Covid symptom. Took test then went to emergency. Worst experience ever considering how seriously health professionals are advising us to take this pandemic. Thankfully ok. Will not return to this hospital unless an ambulance takes me so staff will have no excuse to ignore me or send home and say come back if symptoms grave.  Watched staff kick out pregnant girl and boyfriend because he went and asked for a blanket for her. Said he could no longer wait with her even though she mentioned having some serious anxiety problem. Feel ashamed I kept quiet and out of the situation because afraid they would ask me to leave too. Recognize the staff here are dealing with a lot because of this pandemic, but also noticed some people had more than enough time to socially talk with police officers that were watching a guy handcuffed to a bed. As a minority, think the bad attitude of a few bad apple police are rubbing off on the people working in your emergency. This is a troubling sign if not addressed at a hospital like yours which I consider one of the better health care facilities in the city.

I left there feeling very well taken care of and all my concerns were relieved.  I wish the female dr would have done this blood test and I would not have had to have gone back to emerge a couple nights later.

input: I waited over six hours for my son to be seen for the Doctor to spend about three minutes with us and rush off.  He said he came prepared with the paperwork even before he started so that means he was advised to what my son had prior to the start of his shift.  I am aware that there are more urgent cases and I know I took him to the emergency room but, shouldn't the time of care to assess and treat a patient also be taken into consideration when in an emergency room?  I wouldn't have gone to the emergency room but had no other alternative, the secretary at his pediatrician's office wouldn't book an appointment in the office or phone without my sending a picture of the issue being taken and uploaded onto their app. The app didn't work and the cyst was getting much larger by the eye and he said it hurt.  Also, the doctor said he would prescribe my son an eye ointment to treat the infection but then prescribed a liquid medication intended for a small child, not taking into consideration my son's age and weight, he should have been prescribed tablets.  I was not happy about was inconsistency with the medication prescribed and what was discussed.  Not happy with this visit but I like XXXXXXXXX and the work it does overall.

input: I went from the ER to 3T to 2C. 2C Cardiac was wonderful and amazing and the staff were engaging and fantastic. 3T was a bit of a disaster. It was a temporary wing that had been in place for 7 YEARS and then I get put there because I am 'ambulatory' - while the lady right beside me was NOT ambulatory and used a commode in an open wing with so many people there for different reasons. I asked for a transfer to semi private or private which was granted quick quickly. The staff at 3T were pleasant and helpful but absolutely overworked in a small ward of chaos. I felt like I was in a third world country. My move from the ER should have been coordinated between and I should have been put right to 2C as I was admitted for cardiac reasons. That part was disorganized.

So maybe some more consideration and maybe some tests should be able to be done by a nurse or a triage nurses such as a blood test. I'm just thinking of patients with appendicitis for example.

input: I would appreciate a response to my concern XXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX or XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX My appointment with the doctor at the XXXXXXXXXXX whom I had been seeing for years was on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. At that appointment, her recommendation was that I start taking Prolia. I had the first shot on XXXXXXXXX. By the weekend, I was experiencing significant pain in my left leg such that I was limping, had great difficulty managing stairs and had to use a heating pad at night for the pain. I thought I had pulled a muscle but when it got worse, I went on the internet to research the side effects of Prolia and discovered that my pain was in fact a side effect of the drug. Needless to say, I was scared not knowing what was going on. I called the XXXXXXXXXXX on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and left a voicemail message for the doctor to call me, waited several days but no response. On XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX I called back and this time I was able to talk to a receptionist. She said the only thing she could do was send an email to the doctor and ask her to get in touch with me. She did not know where she worked other than XXXXXXX when she was in the XXXXXXXXXXX. Again, I waited over a week with no response. Knowing that the doctor would be in the clinic on XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, I called back, talked to the receptionist and she left a message for the doctor to call me. She returned my call some three weeks after I had the shot. She had not received either the first message or the email. Fortunately by then I was improving but it was very frustrating to not be able to talk to anyone who could help me. I would recommend that all receptionists know how to get in touch with all of the doctors in the clinic outside of clinic hours. To not be able to get any answers for 3 weeks is absolutely unacceptable and systems should be put in place to prevent a recurrence.

input: I was in ED after brought in by the ambulance ignored for over 3-4 hours stomach filling up with blood. I told them I could not walk or stand up could not get on the bed. They said the doctor would not see me or treat me unless I was on the bed. I called the ambulance because I could not walk or my friend would have taken me in the care. I asked for a bedpan and never got it and they said to wait for the painkiller to kick in in 10 minutes then go. I tried to walked to the bathroom and fainted then they treated me like I was in pain and started treating me properly and asked how I was doing. It was very bad experience. I know some fake it but they need to find the compassion not tell me to wait for 10 min when I am begging for a bedpan.

input: It is a very noisy hospital stay. One can hear all the other patients call bells quite loudly. The 'anti baby theft' alarm is also extremely loud (with good reason); it went off 3 times during our stay and interrupted every opportunity for sleep that we had. We thought that was an excessive amount of noise, especially when it would ring for a while. We actually stayed in room XXXX for our first son and did not set off that alarm once because the nurse told us to stay far away from the brightly marked boundary line. So, with that being said, we suggest the admitting nurse put stress on staying away from the boundary line on the floor as a respect for other patients/families. Also, perhaps patients and families can be advised to use their cell phones in the pre-natal room at the front of the unit or in the hallway as opposed to walking up and down the hallways talking loudly late at night.   Other than that, the staff on the Labour and Delivery unit are amazing and we really appreciated their care and support through the birth of our second child. Thank you.
