input: The nurse in the recovery room, XXXXXX I think was her name, showed me an excellent care, beyond my expectation. She did not mind when my stay in the recovery room was extended due to the late decision to stay overnight after the surgery, breast cancer, and she made sure that I was settled comfortably in the room on the It was quite late that I finally got the room on the , at around 9:30 pm, but she stayed with me all the way until I settled in. I cannot express enough of my gratitude. On the other note, the wiring process before the surgery was quite painful. I was already nervous about the surgery, and this wiring process was the worst part of the whole procedures. I wish I had some better freezing done, even sedation if I had known that it will take that long and give such pain. However the nurse helped me a lot and gave me a gentle care.

input: I found the clinic staff working to lead people to their appointment very helpful and professional. - There is clearly a problem with the ultrasound technicians though. In the past year I got two different technicians and both were pretty rude, did not care if the probe was hurting me and would never make me feel comfortable. I felt I was in front of robots who hated their jobs. There could be improvement to make sure the patient is comfortable (and not just physically comfortable) while there is transvaginal ultrasound. - At XXXXXXXXXX's it seems that the different clinics do not communicate with each other so if you have one test for different matters, you will have to have separate appointments to get the results with several specialists. I wish I could have got the results all at once so I did not have to come back another time to the hospital during the same week (with check in + wait + appointment). What about getting the results by email or mail and get an appointment only if it is really needed? - On the other side, doctors were always excellent and very caring which to me is essential.

input: As feedback for improvement, I would like to report experience of my XXXXX XXXXXX XXXXXXXXXX procedure performed on XXXXXXXXXXXXX at XXX On XXXXXXXXXXXXXX, after my MRI when I went for admission to surgical unit, the behavior and handling of the front desk (male) attendant was very rude. My father was accompanying me primarily to discuss the procedure with the performing doctor, as no one contacted us prior to that to discuss and explain the risks and benefits of the procedure and secondly as I was not steady on my feet due to illness/weakness and effect of XXXXXXX medications The attendant was not only rude verbally, but he came out of his cubicle to physically challenge my father in the best interest of my treatment, my father sustained all the abuse and didn't create any confrontational situation my father was assured that operating doctor will call him and discuss the procedure over the phone. On this assurance, my father went back, leaving me at hospital The day passed and my father didn't receive a call from doctor Doctor did discuss the procedure with me but since I was under the medication influence and without fully understanding all the details and magnitude of procedure, I trusted my doctor to proceed Later in the evening my father received a call from nurse of recovery room to come and collect your son No specific follow up plan was provided other than a brochure for wound care my XXXX bandage done after the procedure slipped down from actual wound (keeping it exposed). We assumed the bandage is covering the new wound/cut of biopsy done on XXXXXXXXXXXXX, while the exposed wound/cut was from the earlier done biopsy on XXXXXXXXXXXXXX My father did call the surgeon's office for a follow up appointment to check the wound, and he was told there is no need for it. My father had to arrange doctor's referral for XXXX (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) nurse to visit me at home for wound care and sutures removal on third day when the XXXX nurse removed the XXXX bandage, there was no wound/cut under it the XXXXXXXXXXXXX biopsy was performed on the same wound/cut made during my 1st biopsy of XXXXXXXXXXXXX After two weeks, when sutures were removed by XXXX nurse and some sutures were not clearly visible (XXXXX XXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXX) and hence, not removed later, when my father contacted surgeon's office, he was told that those sutures were not self-dissolving and should have been removed completely. The way my XXXXXXXXXXXXX biopsy procedure was handled and performed, is a big question on professionalism and responsibility of all those involved. Despite, being more than six (06) months of countless tests, MRIs, CT scans still my treatment for the illness has not been identified I am not criticizing any individual but surely there must be a room for improvement to avoid the tremendous mental stress that I have been put through during my medical treatment.

input: Having a more regular team of nurses caring for my babies. Towards the second half of our stay, we only had one core nurse (who was fantastic) but she only worked nights. So daytime shifts was always rotating and it became confusing and exhausting having to re-explain things all of the time. If one of the nurses gets along well with the family, definitely keep them as a core nurse. The only times we had problems, was when it was a nurse who had not had my twins before and did not know them, therefore, could not provide effective care. Or they ended up being nervous because there was 2 babies.

input: Overall my experience was really good except for the fact when I had my spinal block done for the c section whoever did it obviously struggled because it wasn't done properly. Whoever did my epidural was great and everything went fine that way. My spinal block ended up leaking and I had to come back to the hospital and they said whoever did it had a hard time with it because they caused the issue. It caused me to have severe headaches and caused me to be sick all the time. It caused me to be dehydrated causing me to not be able to breast feed my baby. That was very disappointing. I was sad I had to have the c section but that was necessary and I understood but the spinal block was what caused it to be a bigger issue.

input: Prenatal care was top notch. Not only did Dr. XXXXX and Dr. XXXXXXX take the time to explain things well/ with sufficient detail, they never rushed me through my many questions. The labour and delivery team to me were a dream team ... Dr. XXXXXXXXXX (I got the impression she was up to speed and respectful of the notes my hospital clinic doctors provided), the nurse (she deserves a lot of credit) and the person who administered the epidural (his approach appeared to be to measure several times and administer the needle correctly once) were all incredible. I felt well supported physically and mentally - the team provided ongoing words of encouragement, were very positive and appeared to have high EQ. Only things that could have gone a little better is that during administration the staff lost us for 2 hours (ie. we were shown to the labour room almost immediately which was amazing, however nobody came to see us until 2 hours later after I received a call from staff asking where we were). Two nurses came to cover the nurse that was assigned to me during her breaks. The first nurse tried to convince me to wait until my nurse returned to get started on the epidural which led to an unnecessary delay in pain management. The second nurse that covered a break did not register when I told her that I was bleeding and action was only taken when the nurse assigned to me came back from her break because when I mentioned it to her (the nurse covering did not convey the information so it seems she did not take note of the bleeding) she then took immediate action and called the OB. Moments later I was pushing. The only other thing that I feel could have gone better was getting sufficient care to ensure that my baby was latching properly for breastfeeding. Unfortunately I didn't see the lactation consultant until just a few hours before being discharged. This resulted in me leaving the hospital with quite a bit of breast pain. The hospital still did a great job despite the significant challenges brought on by the pandemic and the overall care was top notch from prenatal care through to labour/ delivery. Thank you, I'll always be grateful for this.

input: Overall, the care we received on this day from nurses, doctors and child life specialists was very good/excellent.  My main feedback would include the incredibly long wait time for anaesthesia for a CT scan.  Our stay was well over 16 hours (an incredibly long time for a toddler).  Communication between doctors/nurses and patient could have also been enhanced.  There were several times where results had not been shared until asked for as well as the status of certain tests and procedures.  Lastly, given the current situation with Covid protocols, perhaps some consideration can also be given to fully vaccinated parents/guardians/caregivers presenting no symptoms.  It was very challenging to deal with the day's events independently.  Both parents should be permitted to be present to assist their child and each other.

input: Tragically, this patient passed away. I see in the letter mailed to our house that I was welcome to complete it. My husband spent the initial portion of his stay in emergency and then in a short stay unit once he was admitted. During his initial stay in mid- XXXX, his symptoms weren't taken seriously and his infection was missed. He returned a week later, as requested, for a follow- up appointment to receive results from those initial tests. At this appointment, the doctor was still unsure what was wrong with him. Yet, less than 24 hours later, someone realized he was septic!! My husband ended up in emergency surgery - which he almost didn't survive - and then placed on life support. Prior to his initial emergency visit in mid- XXXX, he'd been healthy. We are completely dissatisfied with the level of care and attention to his symptoms that he received during the first admission, from both the Emergency team and the short stay team who saw him. We will be following up with that team in due time - right now, we are in shock and grief. My husband spent the remainder of the summer in the Critical Care Unit at both XXXXXXXXXX and then XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (he was transferred XXXXXXX). The level of care we received in the XXXXXXXXXX's CCU was second to none, definitely A+ and we have told them so. We've sent emails to Dr. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, head of the CCU saying as much. We are grateful for all the life- saving and surgical work they did to try to save my husband's life. We speak highly of this medical team and know how hard they worked. The collegiality and expertise of the entire CCU team was impressive and made a big difference for my husband, myself, our kids and the rest of our family who was visiting. The other team who initially saw my husband dropped the ball in more ways than one. Massively disappointing to say the least. That's an understatement. Their miss ended up being fatal for my husband. He was only 41. The discrepancies and stark difference in the level of care my husband received in this two units made it difficult to complete this survey.

input: My leg pain stabs me so sharply that my leg buckles + gives me great difficulty doing simple tasks.  I therefore expected treatment greater than the bare minimum that I received which was simple strengthening exercises.  I expected to receive some sort of deep light therapy, 10's treatments or some other such electronic devices. As for the privacy question. Curtains afford NO sound privacy when discussing personal issues.  #8 - I waited 10 to 15 minutes every appointment after my name was announced over the PA system; while I watched every other patient being met by their therapist within 2-3 mins at the most  I feel my time was not respected tho it is clearly listed as one of the promises to patients posted throughout the physio dept.  I don't recall what the actual name is for the list of promises.  Thank you.  XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXX

input: I was scheduled to have both cataract surgeries done at XXXX. I met the surgeon for the 1st time 2 months before surgery. I specifically asked him if my weight would be a factor in not having the surgery @ XXXX (based on the experience a friend had for the same surgery @ XXXX). I was assured there would be no problem for me. However, 2 weeks before the 2nd scheduled surgery, my surgeon received a message from XXXX that they had cancelled my next surgery due to my high BMI. My surgeon had to schedule my 2nd cataract surgery @ XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX in XXXXXX. I am extremely annoyed that this was NOT determined well in advance of my 1st surgery. XXXX does not have a pre-op assessment for cataract surgery patients & they should have, so that this type of thing would never happen to anyone else in the future.

A lot of the stuff I learned I was not supposed to eat because my clogged arteries were actually fed to me in the hospital.

input: There has to be a level of care which releases the doctor for the most critical patients and allows a patient to be dealt with quickly and efficiently The EMS personnel created a profile for a potential heart attack. You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: Complaints 1. Patients should be consulted before being placed in a ward for "confused" patients, as I was. 2. Visitors should not be asked if the patient is usually mentally deficient without the patient's permission. 3. Where possible women should be in a ward with other women, at least one. 4. Maintenance work should be done in the day - I was kept awake by a light being fixed 5. Patients should not have visitors during the night - a wife talked unnecessarily from 3 am onwards keeping me awake. 6. Patients leaving should not be forced to wait for a wheelchair to park, to watch videos etc. for hours. Agency nurse in charge but did nothing. The staff nurses and doctors were wonderful both surgical and people skills were amazing. XXXXXX noticed my ECG monitor printout was going crazy because of atrial fibrillation and acted quickly.

input: The doctor almost killed me. When he was doing my gastro BI pass he had put in an extra stitch. I was internally bleeding for 6 hours. No one knew what was going on and I was in so much pain. My oxygen was low and blood pressure was up. During my second surgery they had one IV to do the blood transfusion and I only received 2 units. The other arm had 2 IV's and wasn't really into my vein and was going into my arm. The reason I gave the nurses a bad review is when I told the nurse about my swollen arm she didn't take it out until the next day. The catheter then gave me a UTI because of how they put it in. Because of the second surgery I had they had to put a JP on each side. the whole was bigger on one side then the other I was leaking blood. Because the nurse came in and changed. with ought gloves I then had to do several STD test to determine if my blood was safe. I believe that was the nurses fault and not my own and shouldn't of had to be embarrassed IN front of everyone like that.

input: Very inconsiderate. Close to 13 hour waiting with being able to see or talk to anyone. In excruciating pain. And when I tried to talk to someone the male nurse came in my room to tell me the doctor is busy and they know what is wrong with me yet I don't get any help. Just leave me in pain for hours if not it seems like days. Would have been better off dying at home. Cruel and inhuman better off going to a vet, at least I would have got treatment. This hospital is horrible and it's a disgrace to be Canadian. I am embarrassed to say the least. I have worked my hole life and pay taxes to find out these lazy health care providers are sucking up all our money to do nothing. Lazy staff. With there was more oversight. And wish they were held responsible for there actions. I wish I could go to work and do nothing or help who I want. Nice to be able to pick and choose who you want to help. And the way these nurses talk to patients is horrible no respect yet they expect respect. Please call me to discuss. I can go on and on. Can't get the proper test done even when I have an idea of what test should be done. Instead they continue to order the same test that don't show anything. And if I really had nothing wrong do you think I would be in the ER? I have much better things to do. And I'm about to lose my job over this yet I can't get help. And family doctors are just as bad. Every time I call my family doctor it's a minimum three weeks wait. Then you wonder why some patients done care anymore well that's why. Because they can't get any help anywhere in this city. XXXXXXXXXXXX

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

input: I sprained my ankle badly and sought treatment on XXXXXXXXX. It was only in a follow-up visit to the family doctor's office, and when I raised the query with a nurse practitioner who saw me, that I was encouraged to go to a physiotherapist for treatments. Fortunately I have gone and the ultrasound and massage treatments have helped a lot. The young male emergency doctor quickly stated that the x-rays indicated no fracture and to just start walking and that I did not need any sort of brace or further treatments. I had to make another visit to the XXXXXXX on XXXXXXXX, as I had an ear infection and felt as if I had a UTI. The doctor was very professional, but I was first kept waiting a long time in the waiting room. The young man checking me in made an error and crossed off my name and went on to three more patients who were taken in before me. When the error was discovered I received no apology from either him or the admitting nurse who I inquired with as to why I was left unattended.. Thank you for the opportunity to give this input and hope that it helps improve services.

input: This patient has dementia so hard to answer the questions. Because of Covid I (his wife) was not permitted to visit or assist in his care. I was not told when he was moved to a room (only found out when I phoned). When he was moved to his room his CPAP machine was not sent to his room - I had to request someone to go look for it. I told the emergency room staff that he always rips out IV's (and he did twice during his stay) and that even though he had a catheter he would try to get out of bed to use the bathroom so they did use an alarm bed. I understand the constraints because of Covid but only information I received was as a result of my phone calls. Perhaps would be helpful to have liason person/s who can advise family of pertinent info especially in patients with dementia ie moved to a room, take phone to patient to talk with family etc. Aside from that I think this hospital delivers excellent care and is one of the reasons we chose to move to XXXXXXXXXXXX

input: Dear XXXXXXXXXX  My name is XXXXXXXXXX, I was previously a colon cancer patient.  I no longer have cancer but as a result of all my surgery and treatments en d up in the emergency a few times a year because of bowel obstructions.  During my last visit to the emergency it was extremely busy and I ended up having to wait in the triage for more than 3 hours.  During that time I was vomiting and unable to consume liquids or foods due to my bowel obstruction.  As a result I ended up having severe dehydration and my body ended up having severe spasms.  During my obstructions I also experience extreme amounts of pain.  I do have a request and was wondering if patients in a similar situation as mine be provided by IV fluids and pain medication in the triage, especially during the busy times where patients with similar situations as me have to wait for multiple hours.  Just to note, this is not a complaint, I am very lucky and grateful to have ben treated at XXXXXXXXXX.  This is just an inquiry in order to avoid situations like this in the future.  Thank you!

input: For the most part, the care I received by the delivery room nurses was exceptional - I felt very supported and cared for by them. I found there to be a significant difference between the quality of the care given by the delivery nurses and those that cared for me post delivery. I also really appreciate the friendly, humorous, and personable approach by the delivery doctor and appreciated being able to meet with the lactation consultant the day of delivery who provided invaluable information that helped me post hospital. While my OB did not delivery my baby, I really appreciated that he came to visit me the next morning in hospital. I felt that more newborn supplies and supplies for mom with bleeding could have been provided for while at the hospital.

You are a strict multi-label classifier for Social Determinants of Health (SDOH).

Goal:
- Identify labels only if the patient comment reveals underlying life circumstances or social factors
- These factors do not have to have direct impacts on health or current medical care, but should reflect ongoing social conditions affecting the patient's life
- DO NOT label issues that arise solely from current medical care, treatment, discharge instructions, surgery effects, temporary recovery, hospital processes, or wait times.

Allowed labels:
financial-constraint, living-condition, transportation, education, employment-status,
social-connection, violence-abuse, disability-status, physical-activity, substance-use,
sexual-activity, discrimination, no_sdoh

These are the definition for each label:

- financial-constraint: A state of limited, uncertain, or unstable access to sufficient financial resources to meet current and ongoing needs such as housing, food, utilities, and medical care.
- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
- "It's a very long 2-hour bus ride to the hospital." -> transportation
- "After surgery I couldn't drive for 3 days." -> no_sdoh

They took out 1.5 litres that day which is not accurate According to my dry weight. They later called the next day and apologized for this mistake  and said that the nurse that was looking after me was busy with other patients and so another nurse without checking me just released me. I later got home that day and as usual tried to go upstairs and  ended up fainting and falling. My family called 911 and I ended up at XXXXXXXXX.  I tried to explain the situation , but instead of looking at the notes. They just ran some tests, and released me. After a week I got a letter in the mail saying my license has been canceled due to lack of consciousness which I have no history of!  I am now trying to find a doctor at XXXXXXXXX that will fill out the form for MTO and at my dialysis unit they are just giving me the run around. It's extremely frustrating when you do this to a patient ... especially when it's your health unit that made the mistake ... and caused this situation. My cardio said there is nothing wrong with my hearth monitor that I had on for 48 hours ... Dr. XXXXX has my records.  So Some needs to fix this ASAP.  You can reach out to me XXXXXXXXXX.  This is a great hospital.  It saved my life! But  this issue is a big problem for me to get to dialysis !  So I need help.

input: My experience was very good. Totally different from my experience with my mother a few months earlier. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Canadian Patient Experience Survey I received and completed the recent Canadian Patient Experience Survey. My experience was very good, but I need to share the experience with my mother a few months earlier. My mother was XX, feel and broke her hip. Surgery went fine, but things quickly deteriorated. My mother's first language was not English, she was nearly deaf and in the early stages of dementia. Needless to say, with the drugs, communication problem etc. she would not appear very cooperative,. After only one day, my impression was that the staff looked at her and made the decision to send her back to the nursing home and put her in palliative care. She was taking up a valuable hospital bed. Having broken her other hip 6 years earlier, the family knew that she would hallucinate for 2-3 days, and would not be herself. The family was not sure how she would respond to therapy, but she did quite well with time. Her treatment during that stay was good, and we had something to compare the recent stay to. That is why I was shocked to see such poor care/attitude this time around. She was restrained in her bed and we accepted that she needed to be. We spoke to one nurse and mentioned that her nursing home ahd a 'no restraint' policy. The nurse response was 'find another nursing home' Hospital staff wanted my mother out of the hospital within 48 hrs of her operation. They communicated with the nursing home to arrange a transfer. The information that they provided to the nursing home was very limited and selective. Eventually the nursing home staff told the hospital staff that the home was not equipped to take care of her ie. the medication, I's restraints etc. The hospital reluctantly agreed. The transfer waited a few more days for my mother to go off the medications. This at least allowed us the time to see if she was being 'uncooperative' because of her medications (hallucinations), and to make an informative decision. In summary I was left with the following impression. "She's old, not cooperating (ignoring the fact that she didn't understand and could be hallucinating), she is reaching her expected hospital stay time, we can use the bed for another patient. let's get her out of here and have someone else look after her." I realize that the staff couldn't do very much with her, but the general attitude was horrendous and not acceptable to me. This was totally opposite to her first experience my recent experience.

input: I have to say, I don't agree with the revised visitors policy. I understand that studies may show that patients heal faster if they are allowed to have visitors throughout the day and night; however, this can be very disruptive to other patients, especially if you are in a semi-private or ward room. I spent two days in Surgical Observation Unit and my roommate had an excessive amount of visitors all day and night who made a lot of noise and would take up so much space in the room that the orderly couldn't deliver my food tray. The problem is some ruin it for everyone. a How can a patient recover if they are unable to rest. Also, I spent four days in Surgical Unit 1A and that ward is infested with cockroaches. Every time I got up to use the washroom at night and I would open the light, I saw them scurrying across the floor. PLease take care of this problem ASAP. Also, I experienced serious blunders with my medications while I was admitted following major debulking surgery. I requested an epidural for pain relief. I woke in the recovery room and the epidural had not been set up (the line had been inserted but the pump had not been set up). I had an epidural with my previous debulking surgery and I woke up with the pump in place and already numbed. Also, at my pre-op clinic appointment, my medications were reviewed and listed in the hospital system. For some reason, my SSRI drug was not included in the orders and I was not provided with this drug for four days until i was able to take it myself. As a results, I experienced some significant side effects associated with withdrawal which made the following days after my surgery absolute hell. This shouldn't have happened. When I mentioned it to the nurse, she shrugged and said, 'it's not on the orders.' End of story.

input: Our child was not seen by a doctor as the wait times were extremely excessive and there wasn't even a chair available for us to sit in, in the waiting room. We ended up sitting on an end table with our X year old and were told it was going to be a 5 hour wait. We opted to risk going home and not having our child looked at because we figured we could get an appointment at our pediatrician's practice the next morning, faster than being seen at 'emergency' and not risk exposing our child to some other virus in emergency ... Overall I was not impressed with the service we received at an 'emergency' facility that night.

input: Letter to editor is product of stay Dear Editor After reading the health issue article by Mr XXXX it prompts me to communicate my latest adventure regarding our public health system This past week saw me experiencing the latter first hand through spending several days at the local hospital My experience is not one of victim as sometimes prompts letters to the editor Rather it is one of admiration of those who so effectively dealt with my personal situation from triage to residency to release It is the people who deserve recognition and our respect They make the system function admittedly with the help of much technology New devices will undoubtedly further support their efforts but I sense that it was their personal care that contributed most to my wellbeing I thank the approximate twenty individuals with whom I had a capacity to converse and appreciate their dedication to their professions and to me as a patient Keep up the fine effort The human and person touch is very important Respectfully

input: Basically, my care during my stay was very good, but there were a few  exceptions where I was not treated well. Three days after my surgery (XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) my catheter was removed and I had difficulty using the urinal. The problem was that I couldn't get out of bed without some help and using it while still in bed was most difficult to control where urine went. While using the urinal in bed, I wet my gown, sheets and blanket. I called for help, got an immediate acknowledgement of my call but nobody came to assist me. I called 3 times and nobody came. After 50 minutes I started to get angina pains (I have heart blockage) and reported this. Only then did a nurse come to me and it was not my nurse. She was very nice to me but told me she could not comment because, not being my nurse, she didn't know the situation. I might add that I received very little attention from the day staff the entire XXXXXXXX. I am not a demanding person but I do believe that to have to wait 50 minutes after having wet the bed is too long and not acceptable. My nurse's excuse that she was on break does not, in my opinion, justify nobody coming.

- living-condition: Circumstances related to the safety, stability, adequacy, and affordability of one's housing and surrounding environment, including experiences of housing instability, homelessness, or inadequate housing.
- transportation: Uncertain, limited, or no access to safe, reliable, accessible, affordable, and socially acceptable means of transportation necessary to maintain health, well-being, or livelihood.
- education: The attainment of formal education and literacy skills necessary for employment, health decision-making, and daily functioning, including having less than a high school education or limited health literacy.
- employment-status: Access to stable, safe, and adequate employment that provides sufficient income and benefits; retired status is included only when it affects financial stability.
- social-connection: The structural, functional, and quality aspects of an individual's social interactions—including social networks, support, isolation, perceived loneliness, and barriers such as language limitations.
- violence-abuse: Exposure to physical, sexual, psychological, or financial harm, coercion, or neglect within relationships of trust or intimacy, including intimate partner violence or elder abuse.
- disability-status: A physical, sensory, cognitive, or mental impairment—including conditions such as significant pain, allergies, morbid obesity, or temporary wheelchair use—that limits daily functioning or participation in life activities.
- physical-activity: Engagement in bodily movement that contributes to maintaining or improving health, physical fitness, and overall well-being; insufficient activity may increase risk for chronic disease and reduced quality of life. 
- substance-use: The use of alcohol, tobacco, prescription medications, or illicit substances in a manner that may negatively impact health, functioning, or social well-being.
- discrimination: Differences in access to resources, opportunities, or care based on personal characteristics such as age, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, or other identity factors.

Instructions:
- Output one or more labels from the allowed list, separated by commas with no extra words.
- If none apply, output: no_sdoh
- Do not invent labels. Do not add explanations. Only return labels.


Examples (format only; content varies):
- "I can't afford my medication." -> financial-constraint
